item.title: Hedge fund Schonfeld shows which hedge fund jobs are proliferating. It's bus dev
item.description:
Schonfeld, the hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, has filed some UK accounts for Schonfeld Strategic Advisors LLP and if you're interested in knowing who they've been hiring at a high level, you will be fulfilled.
Unlike other hedge funds with UK accounts, Schonfeld helpfully breaks down its headcount by function. Since 2022, it has increased its London headcount by 71 people. But some functions have benefitted from proportionately more hiring than others.
As the chart below shows, the function that's grown most during this period is business development </news/hedge-fund-business-development-executive-bde>, which is the exalted hedge fund term for recruiters who hire portfolio managers. Business development professionals are not just recruiters, though. As the head of bus dev at Point72 observed recently <https://pitchthepm.substack.com/p/why-point72-wins-20-years-next-to?utm_source=substack&publication_id=7758668&post_id=217182070&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>, they also see themselves as doing an investing role. It's just that they're investing in portfolio managers, who then invest for the fund.
At the end of 2025, Schonfeld had 20 people working in bus dev in London, up from only six in 2022. This year, it's lost at least one of them - Sameer Buch </news/hedge-fund-millennium-hired-hedge-fund-schonfeld-s-top-equities-recruiter-in-london>- to Millennium.
Schonfeld's London bus devs have then been accumulating London portfolio managers. A net nine PMs were added last year. 25 have been added since 2022. By comparison, trading, risk and standard HR roles have dwindled.
Despite Schonfeld's portfolio manager hiring in 2025, the FCA Register suggests that five portfolio managers left in September (Rastko Miletic, Joseph Bond, Andrew Prentice, Peter Hunt and Sourabh Tripathi). Their departures are thought to follow Manus Baveja's exit to Dymon in August.

item.title: Morning Coffee: 'Dignified' but unexpected pre-Christmas banking job cuts are go. Another accidental email was sent
item.description:
It's Q4, which means that 'tis the season of banking job cuts. The first to shake out the seasonal ornaments is National Australia Bank (NAB), which yesterday made an apparently unexpected post <https://www.nab.com.au/news/nab-updates/nab-simplifying-operating-model-and-alignment-to-customer-priorities>saying that it will be making 2,500 roles or 6% of its staff redundant, of whom 1,500 will go before Christmas.
All these people will be treated with "dignity and respect", said NAB. They will be engaged and consulted with, redeployed and reskilled and given support in their "transition." They will also be given redundancy entitlements according to "applicable industrial instruments," which sounds complicated.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
NAB's cuts aren't really that surprising. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/nab-to-cut-2-500-staff-use-fewer-consultants-and-contractors>notes that NAB already made cuts in its investment bank in August <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-21/australia-s-nab-cuts-banker-jobs-in-institutional-division>, when it combined origination and sales roles and said, "We recognise change can be difficult."
For bankers and traders and bank employees in locations beyond Australia, NAB's new cuts may not seem relevant. But they are the zeitgeist. NAB is cutting to "improve outcomes for customers by reducing duplication and speeding up decision making." It is focusing on "reducing the size of corporate functions. It is "simplifying its operating model." And it's trying to "better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives."
Bloomberg suggests NAB's doing this now because things aren't great in the Australian housing market, where a severe property downturn has weakened demand for NAB's mortgages. Australia is not alone in this. <https://www.fca.org.uk/data/mortgage-lending-statistics>And NAB is not alone in wanting to be a sleeker place with technologically empowered humans who can handle hard change. HSBC, Citi, Standard Chartered, Barclays and others have similar intentions.
Separately, watch what you send by email.
Following the email error at Morgan Stanley </news/morgan-stanley-md-email>, in which MD Mohamed Atmani </news/mohamed-atmani-morgan-stanley> accidentally sent a list of proposed deals and some prices to clients, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/6075e0ec-9116-4de4-84e6-d50b5ed1d47a?accessToken=zwAAAaFUlDTRkc9gdeDskRZN5NOE5tULXtHUeg.MEUCIQDJ1Mj9bVt_d87G8QF5R0OOX5mtK2RNbVtzLQnpJALHkQIgMXemN_Gm_vbJJQfVZPFZEnYZGwfkfTJd-15i-5HrpsE&segmentId=e95a9ae7-622c-6235-5f87-51e412b47e97&shareId=b4e48217-ec88-4b13-8f0a-d3a55c42ee90&shareType=enterprise&syn-25a6b1a6=1> reports that another accidental email was sent by the most senior people at law firm Freshfields.
The Freshfields email concerned an exchange between the firm's global managing partner Alan Mason and its co-head of US corporate and M&A, Ethan Klingsberg. The two men were discussing how they might spin out Freshfields' legal AI unit and Klingsberg suggested they might try “sophisticated investors that are respected by the rest of the investor community for their leadership”, and then added that this “probably” ruled out “Middle Eastern sovereign wealth money”.
The FT says Mason then accidentally emailed the exchange to a large internal distribution list, some of whom took screenshots.
“We apologise unreservedly for a comment made about Middle Eastern sovereign wealth investors . . . the comment does not reflect the position or beliefs of the firm or those participating in that email exchange, and we sincerely regret the offence caused,” Freshfields said in a statement made to the FT on Monday. It added: “We hold our clients across the Middle East in the highest regard and deeply value the longstanding relationships and trust we have built in the region. We have enormous respect for the discerning leadership and global impact of our clients and remain firmly committed to the region.”
Meanwhile...
Finance is full of jobs that are made up of well-documented, routine tasks where completion can be easily tracked. For banks and insurers, these might include roles handling queries from customers or other staff, overseeing approvals for risk, or monitoring technology and operations. Finance also has the highest share of occupations exposed to AI of any industry at 84%, according to the Bank of England. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-opinion-how-will-ai-affect-jobs-the-uk-finance-industry-is-showing-us/?taid=6ad59ba393db840001f32534&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Optiver wants $900m in financing to expand its trading activities. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/high-frequency-trader-optiver-seeks-900-million-debt-package>
Private equity firms have started trying to expense private jets. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/97643fcb-46f8-43dc-b559-c33709f37866?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Barclays traders discovered that it can put total return swaps referencing illiquid private credit loans in the trading book if they make them into a traded position using a matching trade with another counterparty (known as a back-to-back total return swap). It becomes a traded position even though the loan referenced is illiquid. The regulator is not so sure. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/f3127b4f-d33a-4431-acff-021829f3aa72?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Seth Platt is leaving Two Sigma and co-founder David Siegel must now pick his third proxy on the management committee in about two years amidst his dispute with John Overdeck. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/two-sigma-to-lose-top-executive-seth-platt-amid-founders-feud?taid=6ad67ca2f1222300014cf14e&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
The dispute between Overdeck (who runs quants at Two Sigma) and Siegel (who runs the engineers building the trading systems) highlights the difference between the two jobs. “I would liken the trading and modeling to the striker, or the guy who kicks the ball in the goal at the end of the play,” said Overdeck. “Investment management is very much a team sport. I was managing the very offensive end of the field." (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/two-sigma-overdeck-divorce-siegel-d66db008>
HireVue type interviews are susceptible to fraud and interviewees are being asked to do weird things like hold up fingers and provide proof of identity. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/16e1d29b-3680-4712-b8e7-ed4a4125041a?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
HSBC's departing CFO Pam Kaur has worked for 12 CEO's during her career and thinks the speed of changes at HSBC is manageable. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hsbcs-first-female-cfo-pam-kaur-on-40-years-in-finance-stepping-down-and-sewing-her-own-gowns-02a8038c>
Now is your chance to be head of asset management at HSBC. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/hsbc-starts-search-to-replace-asset-management-head-moreau?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261019&utm_campaign=author_20887312>

item.title: London's high yield traders are suffering after Virgin Media left them exposed
item.description:
Working in high yield trading can be a very lucrative business. It can also be a very painful one.
Following this month's descent of Virgin Media O2's bonds into distressed territory, multiple sources say that some banks' European high yield trading desks are nursing large losses.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The banks concerned either didn't respond or declined to comment.
Virgin Media O2's bonds plummeted in early October after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said provisionally that a plan involving Virgin Media joint venture Nexfibre Networks to acquire Netomnia Ltd, could lead to reduced competition in the UK broadband market.
If the Nexfibre-Netomnia deal goes through, Virgin Media will get £1bn of cash to help pay down its roughly £22bn of debt. The CMA is due to make its final ruling on the deal December 15th. In the meantime, Virgin Media's debt is in distressed territory and high yield desks and hedge funds holding the debt are thought to be nursing large losses. If the CMA decides the deal can go ahead, these losses could yet be recovered.
Desks understood to have lost money recently on the so-called "VMED trade" include JPMorgan's high yield desk in Europe; JPMorgan declined to comment. Separately, a senior high yield trader has also left another London bank in recent weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. The reason for his departure is unclear.
High yield desks have made large profits for successful traders in the past. However, JPMorgan’s European high yield business has also seen multiple senior exits in recent years. They include Bhavit Sawjani, whose team at ExodusPoint reportedly lost more than $70m </news/bhavit-sawjani-jpmorgan-hedge-fund> after he left the bank, and Gianfranco Canepa, whose former team at JPMorgan built up a €500m position </news/2022/12/jpmorgan-high-yield-loss> in French grocer Casino Guichard-Perrachon and also bet on Metalcorp, a subsidiary of Monaco Resources Group. Those positions reportedly swung to a loss of nearly $70m after Canepa left.

item.title: Balyasny reshuffled its applied AI team after its head of research moved into trading
item.description:
Even if you're working on cutting edge applied AI in a hedge fund, </news/how-hedge-funds-use-ai> you're not technically front office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>. That doesn't mean you can't make the switch, as one of Balyasny's most senior researchers just proved.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Peter Anderson </news/balyasny-hedge-fund-generative-ai-google>, who was most recently head of research for applied AI at the fund, has now become head of autonomous strategies within its fundamental equities. Anderson joined Balyasny from Google, but briefly worked as a graduate equity researcher </news/i-spent-30-years-in-equity-research-the-job-only-got-harder> for Credit Suisse before going back to school for a machine learning PhD.
Autonomous strategies in a fundamental team seems somewhat oxymoronic. Balyasny didn't respond to a request for comment, but Anderson's role may be focused on taking the fundamental research of Balyasny's equities researchers and translating it into trading algorithms. </news/2023/03/python-algorithmic-trading> The fund has a separate systematic trading division run by Francine Fang.
Balyasny's chief AI officer Charlie Flanagan is also a Google alum and has filled Anderson's role with one more Googler. Balyasny's new head of research is San Francisco-based Gearoid Murphy who was a senior researcher in the tech firm's innovation lab, X (not the app). He most recently was CTO of a project focused on using AI "to reduce waste, fragility, and inefficiency in the global supply chain." Murphy has a PhD in 'evolutionary algorithms' and also worked in the video game industry </news/the-video-game-that-will-prove-you-deserve-a-job-in-commodities-trading>with physics engine provider Havok.
The fund also hired Itamar Kestenbaum in New York. He joined a senior AI engineer and was most recently a senior engineer in the infrastructure team at Meta in New Jersey. Before that, he spent several years working across tech firms in Israel.

item.title: Jane Street employees all have an AI twin that does their knitting for them
item.description:
Investment banks are building digital employees. </news/jpmorgan-bankers-ai>Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>is building 'AI Users.' The big difference is that these users uniquely correspond to each human employee at trading firm. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Speaking on the Signals and Threads <https://signalsandthreads.com/the-changing-craft-of-programming/#whats-left-of-the-craft-011514> podcast over the weekend, Jane Street engineer John Crepezzi said that the firm has built identities through which AI agents </news/how-ai-is-affecting-careers-in-electronic-trading-and-hft> can act, "which are alternate versions of each of the people at the firm." Jane Street engineers code through Claude Code, Codex, or Jane Street's internal coding systems.
This was initially just a security classification so that Jane Street's systems would "apply the right set of rules" when an agent was acting on your behalf "because they know that the caller is an AI version of you." Since then, however, Crepezzi said that the firm has "built other systems that take use of this AI-concept."
One new use case is a code tracking system that monitors what code was written by these AI users </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing> and what was written by a human. Crepezzi didn't mention other use cases, but said the AI user structure is "show[ing] up in a bunch of other places too."
One of the ways that these users are called into action is through Jane Street's internal slack. Agents will start a project when prompted via chat and start writing the code for it without having to be prompted. Crepezzi said that "something like 45% of the total released features" start in this manner.
How is AI changing Jane Street
We've written about how AI is changing Jane Street's famous internships </news/what-interns-at-jane-street-actually-do-from-2022-to-now>. CTO Ron Minsky has said in the past that there's increased focus on reviewing code rather than writing it due to the tendency of AI to write "uncanny" programs </news/jane-street-cto-everyone-knows-python-lots-of-people-aren-t-any-good-at-it#:~:text=It%27s%20not%20just,still%20super%20broken.%22>that look functional but are "super broken." Senior employees are coding less too, but they're not necessarily happy about it.
Speaking on the most recent podcast, Minsky likened coding to "knitting... you're not maybe solving any big ideas, but the craft of putting the code together" is an "artistic" pursuit. Crepezzi said that the focus is now more on "watching the code that it wrote and offering adjustments where you can."
There are benefits too. Crepezzi noted that AI users starting pull requests through Slack saves you from "a lot of toil involved in just creating a new pull request." Minsky said it also gives engineers time to work on the "code that you would’ve never bothered to write at all."
Crepezzi noted that systems design (the big picture stuff) is "still fairly protected." Minsky suggested that it has also become the bulk of work for Jane Street engineers; he was told by a "very strong engineer" that their work was previously 10% "thinking really hard and deeply about what to do," then 90% executing - now, Minsky said that engineer will offload the execution to an LLM and do "another one of those 10%" problems.

item.title: Barclays head of European rates trading is leaving
item.description:
Hamza Hoummady, the head of European rates trading at Barclays, is understood to be leaving the bank.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Barclays declined to comment and Hoummady didn't respond to a request to comment. Multiple sources say he has resigned. His destination is unclear but he's not thought to be joining a rival bank. There are unconfirmed suggestions that he might be working on a new venture involving data centres.
Hoummady rejoined Barclays from Goldman Sachs in 2022. He previously spent 11 years at the British bank before leaving for Goldman in 2018 and was a popular figure there.
Barclays insiders are lamenting Hoummady's disappearance. It comes after the departure of numerous other members of the macro team, including - most recently James Hackett </news/another-rates-md-left-barclays-in-london-after-resigning-earlier-this-week>, an MD in sales - for a destination that remains unknown.
It's conceivable that Hoummady is joining a fund. London macro funds have ejected quantities of portfolio managers after a troublesome time in 2026, and have seats to fill.
It's not clear who will do Hoummady's job at Barclays. Punitha Raja </news/punitha-raja-barclays> is flavour of the year, but is in sales and is only a director. Guy Winkworth is a possibility. Mark 'The Whale' Wade joined </news/barclays-hired-the-whale-from-nomura> recently, but is comparatively junior. Or Barclays could hire one of the many macro traders to have left a fund in recent months. There's plenty of choice, including the array of senior people who've left BlueCrest. </news/leaving-bluecrest-macro>

item.title: Ex-Citi trader out at hedge fund Capula appears to be leaving after three months
item.description:
It is a bad year to work in a macro hedge fund in Europe. European government bond traders from banks who tried their hands at macro trading in funds are disappearing from their new seats. They are thought to include one former Citi trader who only - finally - joined a hedge fund in the summer.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Multiple sources say that Michele Beretta, </news/capula-hedge-fund-hiring> a former European government bond trader at Citi in Paris, who joined Capula Investment Management a few months ago, is leaving again. The FCA Register shows Beretta arriving in July and exiting the London entity on October 15th. He's still thought to be employed there for the moment.
Beretta didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Capula declined to comment.
Beretta joined a pod at Capula that was run by Andrea Casulli, an ex-Goldman Sachs and UBS rates trader. The FCA Register shows Casulli himself leaving at the end of July 2026.
In the year ending March 2025, Capula's London hedge fund partners were paid </news/capula-hedge-fund>an average of £7.8m each, down from £10.5m in 2024. The average employee there earned £435k last year.

item.title: Optiver hired a partner from hedge fund Rokos in London
item.description:
Chris Rokos of Rokos Capital Management may be on his way out of the UK, </news/chris-rokos-departing-hedge-fund-manager-is-not-just-a-330m-tax-payer> but some of his hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>'s most senior people seem intent on sticking around. Andrius Jankunas, a partner at the firm who joined in 2018 </news/2018/11/rokos-hiring-quants>, has resurfaced with an electronic trading firm's </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>London office.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Jankunas joined Optiver as its global head of quantitative modelling and strategy. He held the same role for Rokos throughout his tenure there. Before that, Jankunas spent just shy of two decades at Goldman Sachs, holding a number of senior roles in its quant strat </news/strats-jobs-investment-banks>division. He was latterly EMEA and Asia head of commodities strats, but also held senior roles in credit, equities and fixed income trading.
Jankunas spent the last two years out of the market while sitting out a noncompete period. This may soon be a thing of the past; Andy Burnham's UK government is planning to reform the labour laws surrounding non-competes, <https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-plans-to-announce-ban-on-workers-non-compete-clauses-in-push-for-growth/> much to the chagrin of hedge funds. </news/internal-audit-citi-consent-order>
Optiver didn't respond to a request for comment, but it seems a particularly senior role to place in its London office. The trading firm is headquartered in Amsterdam, and has growing offices in both Chicago and New York. Its London office has been growing steadily for years, but it seems like a secondary location for the firm, with even the likes of its Sydney office offering greater average compensation last year. </news/optiver-raised-pay-to-591-5k-in-london-but-other-people-earn-much-more>

item.title: The video game that will prove you deserve a job in commodities trading
item.description:
If you're looking for a job on a trading desk, </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> there's an abundance of resources available to help you pass behavioural interviews </news/goldman-sachs-interview-questions>. Surviving the practical tests is another matter. One ex-intern of a commodities trading house </news/commodities-trading-houses> has built a free-to-play video game </news/2023/03/video-game-software-developer-hedge-fund-high-frequency-trading> to fix that.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Deacon Larson, a University of Southern California student, has released a video game titled 'Crude Desk' based on trading simulations commodities firms use to test applicants during their interview processes. You play a junior trader </news/traders-and-brokers> who supports the head of a trading desk while rising the ranks. The game starts out simple, but adds increasingly complex mechanics on each new level that increasingly force you to make decisions under pressure. Mechanically, it's like the trading equivalent of Papers Please. <https://store.steampowered.com/app/239030/Papers_Please/>
Larson, who previously interned at metals trading firm Gerald Group, said the game is not fully accurate as he "simplified the mechanics to make the fundamentals more accessible to beginners while maintaining the fast-paced, challenging nature of trading simulations."
You can play Crude Desk here <https://crudedeskgame.com/>. It also has a leaderboard, which you can use to stake your claim as the next Yaoyao liu. </news/yaoyao-liu-trader>

item.title: Morning Coffee: Exceptional ex-Goldman Sachs trader has big friends and awkward enemies. Princeton PhD ghosted for frozen crab cake job
item.description:
Yaoyao Liu is a 39 year-old oil trader who used to work for Goldman Sachs. </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> He is the sort of person that important people really like and say glowing things about. He also appears to be the sort of person that is observed askance by people with a less favourable opinion of his activities, and who gripe about him.
Liu is one of the biggest traders in the oil market, and has spent the past 14 years working for Vitol. </news/commodities-trading-houses> His big friends have been lining up to express his enormity. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-17/oil-trader-yaoyao-liu-who-made-billions-for-vitol-is-leaving?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261017&utm_campaign=author_22490032> notes that Jonah Van Bourg <https://x.com/jvb_xyz?lang=en>, another ex-Goldman and Vitol oil trader, wrote on X earlier this year that, “Yaoyao is the best trader I have ever worked with," adding. "He is a legitimate 1x/decade commodities superstar.”
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It's not just Jonah. Seb Barrack </news/citadel-energy-trading>, the ex-Macquarie trader running Citadel's huge commodities business has also (weirdly) emerged to praise Liu. “His ability to navigate different regimes and market cycles over many years, combined with his reputation as a significant risk taker, makes him rare among commodity traders,” Barrack informed Bloomberg.
It's not just Johna and Seb. ' Vitol CEO, Russell Hardy, is said by Bloomberg to have been a 'longtime backer' of Liu. Kurt Chapman, the former head of crude at Mercuria, told Bloomberg Liu, “was able to take Vitol to the next level in terms of the derivatives space." Someone else, of unknown provenance, told Bloomberg Liu stood out even at Goldman for his quick mind and ability to grasp complex trading ideas.
We have not spoken to Liu, who graduated from Cambridge University with a first class degree in chemical engineering from Cambridge and who is based in Dubai. We cannot testify whether he is a commodities trader of generational talent. He didn't respond to a request to comment.
Despite his big talents, the WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/star-oil-trader-who-made-wrong-way-bet-to-leave-vitol-6e190ee7> reports that Liu has been sitting out of the market since the summer. He's expected to leave Vitol by the end of the year. People 'familiar with the situation' say this is because he wants to spend time with his family and that he's been planning his retirement since 2025. His awkward colleagues may have played a part in the timing.
As we reported previously, </news/yaoyao-liu-vitol> Liu made some big losses at Vitol, allegedly amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars at one point in 2025. Bloomberg says Liu's team were allowed to continue trading, and ultimately made the losses back. But when Liu's losses swelled again this year, his sceptical colleagues at Vitol appear to have gained the upper hand.
Vitol is owned by employees. In March, the WSJ says some insiders at the trading house raised concerns with Hardy about the size and concentration of Liu's exposure to the oil market. Liu's positions were reportedly then reduced; some were transferred to other desks.
Vitol also didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Nor did Vitol comment to the WSJ or to Bloomberg. Vitol may miss Liu when he finally leaves - he has reportedly made billions in profits for the firm during his time there. Maybe Seb will hire him at Citadel one day.
Separately, if you a Princeton PhD in chemical engineering, are 30 years-old, physically fit and have an encyclopaedic knowledge of history, you will still have to make 2,500 job applications, be ghosted for a job preparing frozen crab cakes, and be unemployed two years after graduating.
This is the situation of Jack Weis, whom the WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/labor-market-freeze-phd-graduate-f8e17d7c?mod=e2tw>reports is hanging out in his parents' basement. When he gets a job interview it involves human-free Hirevue-type interactions and strange psychometric games. Weiss has used AI to design a drone with LED lasers to kill an invasive plant. He's done a bit of work training AI models. He's thinking of going to law school. He's seeing a lot of sperm donation adverts...
Meanwhile....
Perella Weinberg wanted to merge with BDT & MST Partners, but was rebuffed. So then it wanted to merge with the midmarket aura of Piper Sandler and might've called itself “Perella Piper Sandler”, but its senior bankers didn't want that. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/d5a46c91-7e08-4787-806a-c8c43c4ab6c1?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Apollo is taking over EasyJet and it will pay £280m in fees to advisers including lawyers, bankers and public relations groups. EasyJet will pay another £54mn. This will be shared between Barclays, PJT, Citigroup (Apollo) and Simon Robey and Simon Warshaw, and bankers at BNP (EasyJet). (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/66c9bbf1-f25c-4e84-b8ae-c9272fbc49c2?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Two Sigma cut staff in its real estate unit. Rich Gomel, the unit’s partner and chief investment officer, is leaving the firm along with others on the real estate leadership team, including two of the three remaining partners and one of the two heads of data science. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-16/two-sigma-halts-real-estate-unit-fundraising-and-cuts-staff>
Rates traders Colin Bermingham, Philippe Moryoussef, Jonathan Mathew and Christian Bittar can all get jobs in London again. (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/libor-bankers-rigging-overturned-city-fca-t06mvsv0t>
Rachel Reeves tried to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland because of strict new capital rules. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/1bd1cdc2-9dc1-4538-8820-129e9bd9117b?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
If you want a great low cost life you need to be in Valencia. (VisualCapitalist) <https://www.visualcapitalist.com/cp/100-global-cities-by-quality-of-life-and-cost/>

item.title: The Wilderness Diaries, Episode 2: Cutting the Cloth
item.description:
That was it. I was on my own. On a melancholic Monday morning, I woke up with nothing to get up for. Everyone else was squeezing onto public transport. I was at home, and my mind still told me to hurry, that I would be late.
I was not late.
No commute. No coffee, well, coffees, from the usual chain. No dropping shirts at the dry cleaner. No booked class at the gym. No clean shave either. The stubble became de rigueur, and it is relatively trendy these days, I told myself.
What came to mind was a university lecture on household behaviour and James Duesenberry’s theory: people spend according to the standard of living they have grown used to, and resist cutting back when their income falls.
I never found that convincing, at least for me. My first instinct was the opposite. To last as long as possible without a job, my standard of living had to drop.
The most drastic change was cancelling my monthly travelcard, £171. I dusted off my commuter bike, which I still use today, even for the occasional interview. Next went my subscriptions, including a fancy AI one. Another £70 saved. Dry cleaning followed. After all, I now had plenty of time to wash and iron my shirts, albeit irregularly.
Warren Buffett once observed that you only find out who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out. I was determined to keep my trunks on. A few ex-colleagues were not so lucky. More on that later.
It sounded like a tidy cost-saving exercise, but it came at a mental cost. It was not the money I missed so much as the extras: the coffees, the races abroad, the small pleasures that make a week feel normal. I was suddenly staring at survival rather than living, and I wondered whether that would send me spiralling.
Then another idea occurred to me: should I claim Jobseeker’s Allowance? No. A financier does not do that. That was how I felt for the first few weeks. I realised quickly that claiming was not a matter of pride. It was a necessity.
Click here for Episode 1. </news/losing-your-job-in-banking>

item.title: A Goldman Sachs MD found her way home to Morgan Stanley
item.description:
If you work for Goldman Sachs in New York City and you leave for a corporate development job at a crypto infrastructure firm in Miami, then you need not stay in Miami-crypto world forever. There is a way back.
Victoria Hegan, a Durham University graduate who spent 13 years at Goldman Sachs in London and New York, left for a Miami-based role at Fireblocks, a digital asset and stablecoin infrastructure firm, in 2022.
Hegan spent 15 months in Miami before returning to New York banking. Around eight months later, she joined Deutsche Bank in 2024, and was the head of DB investment solutions and commodities distribution for the Americas at the German bank.
Now, though, Hegan has resumed her place in the US top tier </news/the-top-tier-banks-are-goldman-sachs-jp-morgan-and-morgan-stanley-except-for-here>. Having officially left Deutsche Bank in late September according to her FINRA registration, <https://brokercheck.finra.org/individual/summary/6579862>she has now joined Morgan Stanley in New York as head of institutional structured derivative sales for the Americas.
Morgan Stanley declined to comment.
It is a happy ending to the kind of career diversion into crypto corporate development that was popular a few years ago. In 2021, Fireblocks said it was the most well-funded crypto infrastructure provider in the industry. There have been suggestions <https://www.theinformation.com/articles/goldman-jpmorgan-eye-crypto-clients-as-ipo-prospects-brighten> that it will pursue an IPO but this has not occurred yet.

item.title: Citadel Securities hired Aditya Singh from Balyasny
item.description:
Last week reported that ex-Goldman Sachs rates trader Aditya Singh </news/james-watson-balyasny-millennium> had left Balyasny Asset Management.
Today, we can report that Singh is joining Citadel Securities.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Citadel Securities didn't respond to a request to comment on Singh's arrival when asked multiple times last week. We understand that he will be supporting the rates team.
Singh is understood be joining the team run by Nikhil Choraria </news/nikhil-choraria>, another Citadel Securities hire from Goldman Sachs. Initially we were given to understand that Citadel Securities had not hired Choraria, but Choraria arrived there in September and is running the fixed income business.
It's thought that Singh resigned from Balyasny before the recent spate of exits at the fund </news/star-ex-goldman-sachs-trader-retires-aged-33-following-eight-year-hedge-fund-career>, possibly departing in May. Balyasny declined to comment previously on his departure.
Citadel Securities employs a cluster of Goldman's ex-macro people in London. As well as Choraria and Singh, it employs Nohshad Shah, Frank Flight </news/citadel-securities-is-making-its-ex-goldman-sachs-macro-vp-famous> and Ishaan Sethi.
Citadel Securities declined to comment.

item.title: Goldman Sachs employees have quietly had their pay juiced by circa $3bn this year
item.description:
Goldman Sachs </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> does not pay </news/goldman-pay-2026> badly. It does not necessarily pay enough to allow many employees to retire aged 33 </news/star-ex-goldman-sachs-trader-retires-aged-33-following-eight-year-hedge-fund-career>, but accounts filed this week suggest it is on track to pay an average of $476k per head </news/goldman-sachs-jobs> this year in combined salary and bonus.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
There is more to pay at Goldman Sachs than the headline numbers, though.
When Goldman Sachs pays bonuses, it - like other banks - pays some of the bonuses in Goldman Sachs stock, and this stock is deferred over a three year period. If Goldman Sachs' stock rises in price during the deferral period, employees benefit.
Goldman Sachs stock has risen in price a lot. In January 2023 it was trading at around $345 per share. In July 2026, it peaked at over $1,000 per share. Goldman's rising share price has benefitted senior people like CEO David Solomon </news/how-to-earn-100m-at-goldman-sachs>. It has also benefited everyone else with Goldman stock, seemingly by circa $3bn in total.
The $3bn uplift is suggested by Goldman's regulatory filings and its Q3 accounts <https://www.goldmansachs.com/pressroom/press-releases/2026/2026-10-13-q3-results> filed this week.
In a footnote to this week's accounts, Goldman said it received a $975m tax benefit from share awards during the first nine months of 2026. $895m of this was booked in the first quarter.
This tax benefit is the tax that Goldman saved because the higher value of employees’ shares when they were delivered became tax deductible, rather than their lower value when they were granted. If Goldman’s tax rate was around 28%, the $895m saving implies that the share awards had increased in value by around $3bn since they were granted. This money has flowed through to employees in 2026 (although the shares can't actually be sold until next year).
Not all Goldman's 47,500 employees will have benefitted, though. The firm declined to comment for this article and Goldman doesn't say how widely its historic stock bonuses were dispersed. If 20,000 employees received the historic stock, this year's uplift would be $150k each; if 5,000 did, it would be $600k.
This is clearly a fine thing for Goldman's employees. However, recent restricted stock units (RSUs) given to staff at Goldman may be sadly less lucrative.
Filings show that Goldman issued 3.5m RSUs to staff in early 2026 for 2025 bonuses. The price at which these RSUs were granted hasn't yet been divulged, but it was likely between the $930 and $975 at which Goldman's shares were trading in late January. The stock has since fallen to around $925.

item.title: Star ex-Goldman Sachs trader retires aged 33 following eight year hedge fund career
item.description:
It is not easy to retire young in 2026. It is not impossible.
Stanley Sheriff, </news/32-year-old-star-ex-goldman-sachs-trader-poached-by-hedge-fund-balyasny-one-week-into-job>a former star Goldman Sachs junior macro trader </news/2018/03/as-goldman-sachs-hires-in-ficc-some-of-its-best-young-staff-are-leaving>who left for the buy-side in 2018, is understood to have retired from Balyasny Asset Management aged 33.
Neither Sheriff not Balyasny responded to a request to comment.
Sheriff joined Balyasny in Dubai in May 2025. His move to the US fund caused excitement </news/hedge-fund-gardening-leave> because Sheriff had only just joined Taula Asset Management </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>, where he worked for less than a month before Balyasny poached him.
Sheriff's intentions are unclear but he is not thought to be seeking a new role and to be spending some time relaxing. Maybe he will reappear.
Sheriff spent four years at Goldman Sachs from 2014 after graduating with a first class degree from the London School of Economics.
His departure from Balyasny follows various other exits from the firm. As we were first to report last week, Millennium rehired James Watson </news/james-watson-balyasny-millennium>, who was running a 20 person pod in London. Ex-Goldman Sachs traders Aditya Singh and George Tyrrell left too. The FCA Register also shows ex-Symmetry portfolio manager Peter Blandford leaving on October 9th.

Stanley Sheriff, </news/32-year-old-star-ex-goldman-sachs-trader-poached-by-hedge-fund-balyasny-one-week-into-job>a former star Goldman Sachs junior macro trader </news/2018/03/as-goldman-sachs-hires-in-ficc-some-of-its-best-young-staff-are-leaving>who left for the buy-side in 2018, is understood to have retired from Balyasny Asset Management aged 33.

Sheriff joined Balyasny in Dubai in May 2025. His move to the US fund caused excitement </news/hedge-fund-gardening-leave> because Sheriff had only just joined Taula Asset Management </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>, where he worked for less than a month before Balyasny poached him.
Sheriff's intentions are unclear but he is not thought to be seeking a new role and to be spending some time relaxing. Maybe he will reappear.
Sheriff spent four years at Goldman Sachs from 2014 after graduating with a first class degree from the London School of Economics.
His departure from Balyasny follows various other exits from the firm. As we were first to report last week, Millennium rehired James Watson </news/james-watson-balyasny-millennium>, who was running a 20 person pod in London. Ex-Goldman Sachs traders Aditya Singh and George Tyrrell left too. The FCA Register also shows ex-Symmetry portfolio manager Peter Blandford leaving on October 9th.

item.title: The impending boom of compute trading markets: "people are holding their cards to their chest"
item.description:
Are compute markets the next big thing for commodities traders? DRW's Don Wilson believes that GPU </news/programming-languages-machine-learning-ai-quant> compute will surpass crude oil as "the largest commodity in the world," <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HesU-7YJr1Q> and plenty of startups have been building the infrastructure to trade it. Finding traders to participate in those markets is a very different challenge.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Which firms are in the compute trading space?
According to Galaxy Digital, <https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/inference-capital-markets-ai-compute-gpu-futures-onchain-crypto#:~:text=Crude%20oil%20is%20priced%20off%20benchmark%20grades,Price%20Index%20built%20from%20live%20transaction%20data.> there are three primary participants in the compute trading space:
AI labs </news/the-difference-between-working-as-a-quant-in-finance-and-as-a-researcher-in-an-ai-lab>, "the natural buyers," who "have promised capacity downstream and need to secure the input." Hyperscalers, brokers and other firms sitting on "large GPU inventories with uncertain future use." For example, the primary business model of 'neoclouds' like Coreweave </news/brannin-mcbee>is renting out GPU clusters. Prop trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> and speculators, "present in every market where there is an opportunity to make money, [which] sit on top and add liquidity."
The specific firms exploring compute desks are less clear. There are only a handful of public frontrunners: DRW is the most prominent, with Don Wilson co-founding the Compute Exchange at the start of 2025. Jump Trading is the most recent; it hired the founders of GPU trading platform Itô Markets this week to be the heads of its new compute trading desk. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-13/jump-trading-hires-startup-founders-to-lead-compute-desk> Some smaller players are also public; European prop trading firm Vitus Commodities had an open listing last month for a founding quant </news/quant-jobs-finance> trader to build its compute desk in Switzerland.
"People are having a lot of conversations" says David McGuigan of trading recruitment firm Albert Bow, but "people are holding their cards to their chest." Many seem to be at the 'considering' phase. The Information <https://www.theinformation.com/articles/goldman-jpmorgan-explore-new-ways-tame-ai-lending-risks> reported in June that Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan have considered a compute desk. Compute Exchange co-founder Carmen Li (who we spoke to in March </news/trading-gpus>) told The Information that the exchange is "heavily engaged with all the banks." The major AI labs have not said anything publicly, but OpenAI </news/open-ai-outpaid-quant-trading-firms-in-london-last-year-offering-2m-per-head-including-stock>was hiring for a power trading lead in August <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-10/openai-is-hiring-a-power-trading-lead-for-its-data-center-portfolio> to help the firm hedge the risk of infrastructure costs for its data centres.
Like prediction markets, </news/traders-earning-1m-on-kalshi-are-offered-double-or-nothing-to-join-trading-firms>another burgeoning asset class, a lot of trading on compute markets today is done by individuals, mostly in San Francisco. Research <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12156> from Johns Hopkins professor Yinan Su shows that the market is affected by various factors like the scarcity of specific GPUs and the obsolescence of older chips, so San Francisco natives with better understanding of the AI ecosystem have a competitive advantage. McGuigan notes, however, that these solo market makers usually lack "New York quantitative skills to get the pricing right."
Who are they hiring?
The two profiles for compute markets are obvious: AI industry alums with deep understanding of the space, or quants/traders with deep knowledge of commodities pricing. Su told us that a trader "brings financial discipline, while someone who understands AI infrastructure brings valuable technical insight." The ideal candidate is someone who has both; Su said they need to be able to "adapt to this quickly developing market while applying first-principles economic thinking."
This is not a common profile, and even internship experience either side of the divide is seen as very valuable. McGuigan said that one candidate with both AI and quant experience received "11 offers from VCs </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-venture-capital>, hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, family offices and prop firms and he hasn't even finished college." The clearest example of this is Jump Trading's acqui-hire of Itô,. One member of the founding team, Affaan Mustafa, is a San Francisco-based serial founder. The other, Alejandro Soumah, was a quant strat on Goldman Sachs' credit desk in New York.
The ideal trader, you could theorize, would therefore be one of the former high-frequency trading quants that have been lured in by AI labs over the last few years. Junior traders were offered multi-year packages of up to $3m </news/openai-culture> though, so a particularly impressive compensation offer might be required to prompt another move.
Not everyone is looking for that profile. An opening for a compute quant researcher at DRW last month said that "prior exposure to compute or semiconductor markets is not expected and will not be weighted." Commodities trading experience is "directly relevant, though not required." It instead wants people who have the "ability to build a price from structural first principles where market data is sparse or absent." So far, the only DRW employee publicly stating their involvement with compute markets on LinkedIn is Sunny Hu, a former BlackRock trader who has been at the firm since 2023.
The problems
Are Wilson's dreams of compute surpassing oil really that credible? There are several things that hamper its viability as a market. For one, the market depends on companies which investors believe might not survive. Take CoreWeave, one of the largest GPU rental providers, whose stock plummeted roughly 15% over the course of this week before rebounding. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-16/coreweave-stock-wipeout-exposes-divide-between-ai-fear-and-greed> reported that credit default swaps traded for CoreWeave this week priced in a 60% chance of default in the next five years, despite the fact it has “a strong customer base" according to Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick. For now, this isn't affecting rental prices much; Silicon Data's GPU index shows that the price per hour of H100 chips fell this week, but at a much more marginal rate of 1.4% compared to CoreWeave's stock. The price of H200 chips actually rose. However, forward contracts commonly run for three to five years, and if a major GPU provider suddenly exits the market during that period, there could be huge ramifications.
There's also a matter of infrastructure. McGuigan said that "until the exchanges and prices are built properly, the chance for arbitrage is not going to be there." Su's research furthers that claim; cash-and-carry arbitrage strategies aren't viable for compute as an asset because it operates more like electricity than oil in that it cannot be stored. "If the capacity is not used today, today's GPU-hour is lost." Wilson agrees with the comparison to electricity; he told Bloomberg that he sees a world where there are compute futures "for every month, and if you want to hedge the next three years, you sell thirty six of them and now you've locked in your pricing."
There's also potential for market manipulation. The Chicago Mercantile Exchange has been planning to launch compute futures contracts for Nvidia GPU rental prices by as early as this month, but had to delay the launch. The CFTC put out a request for comment in August <https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/21/2026-17163/request-for-comment-on-the-listing-of-compute-derivatives-contracts>in which it stated "dominant market participants may wield significant pricing power that may lead to manipulability, preferential pricing arrangements, and, in turn, unfair market dynamics."
There could also be liquidity concerns. Annanay Kapila, founder of futures exchange QFEX, said he "[doesn't] see a lot of interest in compute trading, especially amongst retail."

item.title: Morning Coffee: The 41-year-old ex-gas trader and the “unlimited” money. Private equity firm cuts jobs
item.description:
Brannin McBee is a billionaire. But as of his interview with the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/4ffa1853-0e2c-424f-b941-88c6bcac5765?syn-25a6b1a6=1> on Wednesday, he is probably worth less than before. McBee is among the founders of CoreWeave, the $39bn "neocloud" provider beloved of places like Jane Street. His comments to the FT came during a week when CoreWeave's stock at one point declined 28% <https://www.wsj.com/finance/stocks/the-riskiest-corner-of-the-ai-trade-is-crashing-into-higher-rates-fcdaad37?mod=hp_lead_pos1>amidst a surge in the cost of insuring against a default on the $35bn of debt <https://www.wsj.com/finance/stocks/the-riskiest-corner-of-the-ai-trade-is-crashing-into-higher-rates-fcdaad37?mod=hp_lead_pos1> that CoreWeave carries on its balance sheet alone. Following this, the WSJ noted that one of CoreWeave's bonds was trading at distressed levels.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
What did McBee say exactly? Several things. Speaking to the FT while wearing trainers (sneakers), bangles and what appeared to be a Patek Philippe perpetual calendar chronograph, McBee said CoreWeave wants its debt to have an investment grade rating so that it can borrow money from insurers whose pockets are immeasurably deep. Their capital, “is unlimited. Like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche,” he pondered.
This appears to have freaked out investors, who were already wondering when the borrowing might stop. The implication is maybe never.
The FT's interview with McBee also suggests that Coreweave is, at heart, a kind of project financing firm. The FT didn't quote him directly, but noted that CoreWeave is a 'financing machine.' CoreWeave owns hundreds of thousands of NVIDIA AI chips and it uses them as security for loans in so-called 'offtake' contracts, under which clients pay to rent GPU clusters that haven't been built yet. “You say, here’s an idea, and then you forward-sell contracts associated with that idea, and you use those contracts with that collateral to go finance it,” declared McBee.
While this happens, the chips sit in subsidiaries. McBee informed the FT that each dollar they earn first pays interest, principal and running costs, with the remaining 20 cents going to the parent. That parent is CoreWeave.
CoreWeave's leveraged project finance vibes have been noted before <https://davefriedman.substack.com/p/how-coreweave-actually-finances-its>. Offtake structures are usually used to finance power plants and McBee is not afraid to point this out. McBee himself helped pioneer the method for financing GPUs, with the help of bankers at Morgan Stanley and MUFG.
McBee knows a few things about energy and power plants because before he found himself a billionaire wearing an apparent Patek Philippe watch, he was a project manager in the energy industry and a prop trader working in the energy sector. Early in his career, he completed a one year internship at McBee Oil Corp in Dallas, suggesting his family might know about the energy industry too.
What now? McBee might not be giving unfettered FT interviews in the future. CoreWeave shares recovered yesterday after Jensen Huang at NVIDIA helpfully declared “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day.” But doubts remain over CoreWeave's debt. What happens, for example, if the NVIDIA chips become outdated and worthless by the end of the contracts? What happens if CoreWeave's customers on short term contracts decide they want to use someone else's data centres instead? What happens if CoreWeave's borrowing costs keep rising?
McBee is untroubled by these questions. Or at least he was, when he spoke to the FT. CoreWeave's debt structure is not "scary debt at all. I look at that as accelerating debt and great debt,” he said.
McBee also observed that he has no intention of riding into the sunset. “We could go off to a ranch and retire,” he told the FT of himself and his CoreWeave cofounders. “But you’re watching us show up every single day and put our time into this business.” It probably helps that the co-founders have already sold $3.3bn <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/coreweave-founders-shield-fortunes-with-3-3-billion-stock-sales>of CoreWeave shares and so are helpfully insulated from what happens hereafter.
Separately, private equity </news/junior-bankers-still-want-to-work-in-private-equity-i-hate-my-life-now-it-s-just-a-question-of-getting-in>jobs have historically been nice steady seats leading to nice steady </news/private-equity-credit-pay> carried interest payments, </news/what-is-carried-interest> but this is no longer so.
Carried interest is harder to get now. </news/leaving-banking-private-equity>And at least one private equity firm is cutting jobs.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/partners-group-is-said-to-cut-jobs-in-its-private-equity-unit?srnd=homepage-americas>reports that Partners Group, a Swiss-based firm with an unfortunate array of deals cut in 2021 and 2022, has been cutting or 'reassigning' dozens of jobs in its private equity division.
In a comment to Bloomberg, Partners Group declared that the size of its private equity team, "remains consistent with its long-term average, while we have significantly strengthened our senior operational capabilities over the past year.” It also said: “This reflects a buyout environment in which creating long-term value and driving distributions require greater operational intensity.”
Operationally intense times require operationally intense hires. Junior bankers maybe less so.
Meanwhile...
CoreWeave debt is priced for a 60% chance of default in five years. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/coreweave-risk-gauge-hits-record-pricing-60-odds-of-default?taid=6ad0ec18e2ba810001fc9cd5&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Deutsche Bank likes CoreWeave. “A confluence of factors appear to have led to a sharp selloff in CoreWeave’s public equity and debt over the past week...we struggle to find company specific factors that justify the recent move.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/coreweave-s-selloff-is-buying-opportunity-deutsche-bank-says?taid=6ad108eccd12f7000141ea41&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Telecom bonds began cracking six months before the dot-com crash. In 2007, subprime mortgage bonds peaked eight months before the S&P 500 did. Equity investors get paid to be dreamers. Lenders get paid not to lose money. (Semafor) <https://www.semafor.com/newsletter/10/15/2026/semafor-business-stress-signals?utm_source=newslettershare&utm_medium=business&utm_campaign=FirstWord#b>
Shares in Société Générale have dropped more than 20 per cent since the start of August, and BNP Paribas has tumbled 19 per cent. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/69bfdf93-cbba-477c-9fb0-5978d1d4f506?accessToken=zwAAAaE_NaCMkc9pv9-Ty7pHfNOfsFl40dT1Bg.MEUCIQDe20Qj04tXVkiCBBAasFNQOJ1ZGoB2tolu2CQPnySHfAIgVUbWE7rRwNDFPNT16UoNqXdbWh9MHHz0HR09YmD7tNg&segmentId=e95a9ae7-622c-6235-5f87-51e412b47e97&shareId=853cb99a-da93-4bd9-8ae0-4c564544a518&shareType=enterprise&syn-25a6b1a6=1>
The British government is preparing to increase the tax on banks from 3% to 8%. The TUC wants a 16% tax and is saying: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits – driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.” (Guardian) <https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-taxes-banks-budget>
Credit Suisse bankers lost their bid to get their bonuses back. The Swiss finance ministry cut bonuses for about 1,000 senior bankers at Credit Suisse. The executive team lost their bonuses entirely. Bonuses for managers one level below the executive board were cut 50%. while employees two levels below had their bonuses cut by 25%. The Swiss Supreme Court said this was fair. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/6607f0e4-6f99-46d1-a994-decafda46e16?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
How it is when you work in AI. 'To seduce a U.S. diplomat in Russia, a foreign espionage operation first sent a blond woman to his hotel room with Champagne. When he declined, the spies sent a redheaded woman, and then next a young man.' (WSJ) < https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/ai-companies-play-cat-and-mouse-with-secret-stealing-spies-160eec6b>

item.title: BlueCrest parted company with an array of senior macro traders hired from banks
item.description:
As we reported a few weeks ago </news/leaving-bluecrest>, people have been leaving BlueCrest </news/bluecrest-mike-platt>, the family office of the legendary macro trader, Michael Platt. </news/what-s-it-like-to-work-for-mike-platt-at-blue-crest-capital-management>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
These exits are thought to include Ben Turner, the 26 year-old ex-Barclays </news/barclays-macro-to-hedge-funds>sterling rates trader who only became a BlueCrest partner on May 1st </news/ben-turner-bluecrest> and whom insiders say was a recent favourite of the firm. The exits also include several other senior macro traders hired relatively recently from banks.
Josh Hooker, </news/2023/09/leaving-deutsche-banks-macro-business> Deutsche Bank's former head of STIR trading, who joined BlueCrest three years ago, is thought to have gone.
We have not spoken to Hooker to confirm his exit and BlueCrest has not responded to requests to comment. However, Hooker was 'terminated as a member' <https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/OC349662/filing-history/MzU1MDQzMDcxNWFkaXF6a2N4/document?format=pdf&download=0>of the firm on Monday according to a filing with Companies House. The FCA Register shows him leaving on the same date.
Francois Puget is also thought to have gone. Puget left BlueCrest's UK entity on October 6th according to the FCA Register. Puget joined BlueCrest in November 2025 and was previously at BNP Paribas for 30 years. He was latterly the French bank's head of G10 rates for Europe. Puget didn't respond to a request to comment.
Eelis Niemelainen, a former MD in EUR rates trading at UBS, also left BlueCrest's UK entity on October 6th according to the FCA register and also didn't respond to a request to comment.
It's thought there may be several other exits too. The reason for the departures is not clear.

item.title: The top tier banks are Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan & Morgan Stanley, except for here
item.description:
What is a top tier investment bank, </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> and do you work for one? Maybe you don't care, but if broad judgements of prestige are important to you, the chart below will be important too.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
If you want to work for a bank that is big and thriving in advisory (M&A) this year, you will want to work for Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan or Morgan Stanley.
If you want to work for a bank that is big and thriving in equities trading this year, you will want to work for Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan or Morgan Stanley.
The same applies if you want to work in equity capital markets (ECM), although it's worth noting Morgan Stanley's ECM bankers floundered </news/morgan-stanley-s-results-suggest-it-was-a-bad-time-to-have-leaked-that-deal-list> in the third quarter and Citi's were on fire. </news/citi-m-a-bankers>
Beyond M&A, ECM and equities sales and trading, though, the waters are muddied.
Citi's fixed income trading business is second only to JPMorgan's and was the only one to grow revenues year-on-year in Q3. BofA's DCM business is second only to JPMorgan's.
The charts obfuscate discrepancies by traded product, region, and banking sector. At this very highest global level, though, only one bank is in the top two for four out of five business areas.
That bank is JPMorgan. It only needs to try harder in equities.

item.title: Bank CEO's wife shares insights on the art of staying married
item.description:
It's not easy to maintain </news/divorce-banking-trading> a 35-year marriage when you work in financial services, but Steven Fine, the CEO of UK-based mid-cap investment bank Peel Hunt, has achieved this.
Fine's wife has been sharing the secrets of their enduring romance.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Speaking on the Instagram account of their daughter, the influencer Gemma Alster <https://www.instagram.com/gemmaalster>, Fine's wife Jacqueline said the rules for a long marriage include: always going to bed at the same time, even if you're not tired; never looking at screens or having a TV in the bedroom so that you are not distracted from intimacy; making time for each other even if you are exhausted. "You have no chance of having a good sex life if you don't make time for each other," Jacqueline explained.
Peel Hunt declined to comment. Peel Hunt insiders say they watch the videos keenly in order to better understand their CEO. Fine himself features in some of the videos, which are also popular on TikTok.
Fine is understood to be relaxed about his daughter's channels and their content. Some Peel Hunt insiders have raised eyebrows about the apparent opulence on display, although this is standard influencer fare.
Peel Hunt paid few bonuses </news/bonuses-peel-hunt-panmure>for three years from 2022, before paying bonuses again this year. For the year ending March 2026, it reduced headcount by 31 people to 267 and spent an average of £269k per head on staff costs. Fine himself received total compensation of £1.4m after a strong year.
Fine's daughter's influencer status is well known in London financial services circles. One competitor observed that Fine seems very vigorous.
Jefferies' CEO Richard Handler </news/2022/01/richard-handler-jefferies> also has a daughter who is active on Instagram and has also been married for a long time. It is not clear whether he allows screens in bed.

item.title: Citi’s new patents for an AI wealth “Avatar” might make its advisors nervous
item.description:
Citi’s wealth business </news/the-coffee-run-andy-sieg-s-rocky-road-to-saving-citi-wealth> seems to have come a long way over the past few years. The unit which made a loss in 2023 has made $1.6bn in net income, for the year to Q3, but it still lags behind the bank's other units like services and banking which have already exceeded their RoTCE targets. To narrow that gap, Citi Wealth is trying to get rid of its historic reputation for having the “worst tech on the street;” <https://www.businessinsider.com/citi-wealth-tech-problems-andy-sieg-2024-6> one way it is doing that is with an AI “avatar” that can perform tasks once reserved for the bank’s wealth advisory staff.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Citi unveiled this concept under the name Citi Sky <https://www.citigroup.com/global/news/press-release/2026/citi-wealth-unveils-citi-sky-ai-powered-member-google-cloud-deepmind-technologies> earlier this year. Since then, Citi has filed multiple patents with the USPTO, <https://www.uspto.gov/patents/search/patent-public-search>* authored by Joseph Bonanno, Citi's head of wealth intelligence, and other Citi contributors. They provide additional details on the scope of these avatars.
Citi’s avatars are a conversational agent with "a representational identity that persists across interactions." These avatars can communicate with clients across different devices (including smart-glasses); responses "can include an audio signal and/or a video signal," and the avatar can use various styles including sign language (Citi said Sky would roll out in English and Spanish only at first). The avatar's responses are influenced by a variety of sources including "investment theses developed by [Citi's] research teams” and "notes documented by an agent during in-person meetings or telephone conversations”
The Citi Sky unveiling showed one such avatar <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GhkLgpJCh9Y>in the generic human style common of conversational agents currently on the market. <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=88qei5nctA0&t=1s> However, there seems to be some flexibility as to how this avatar is presented. It displays visual characteristics such as facial features, body structure, and clothing," and presents information "in a format that resembles human-to-human interaction" but can also appear as "a two-dimensional or three-dimensional animated figure.” Clients can ask for the appearance of this avatar to be augmented but Citi prevents them from having "inappropriate, gory, stereotypical or offensive" appearances, or "uncanny facial expressions" <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trollface>
Citi markets Sky as “always-on.” Patents show that it achieves this by having agents in the background proactively monitor information sources for things that might affect their clients. The patents state this is different from many pre-existing robo-advisors which are "typically user-initiated, stateless, and rule-based."
What does this mean for Citi's human advisors? The patents state that agents can hand off tasks to a human advisor which involve "complex financial instruments" or when regulations “mandate human involvement.” Clients can also express a preference for "human handling of certain action types,", and will be directed to a human when an "action requires personalized advice that exceeds the scope of automated processing."
Humans seem to be important for client origination too, although Citi is putting increased focus on staff outside of wealth to do this; Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citi-wants-bankers-to-introduce-at-least-one-client-to-wealth-unit-by-end-of-2026-425cc201> reported yesterday that investment banking staff are each being tasked with converting ‘at least one’ banking client to its wealth business.
Andy Sieg, in an AI-inspired comment during the Sky announcement, said the tech “doesn’t replace our advisors – it makes them more powerful.” He said the bank also “plans to add advisors in the years ahead.” Still, if Sky proves a success, it may leave many people surplus to requirements as Citi continues to prune itself. They will hope the situation is not similar to HSBC’s UK wealth business; the British bank is cutting as many as 70% </news/hsbc-wealth-cuts> of staff after bringing in AI tools to assist the division.

item.title: Morning Coffee: 24 year-old hedge fund manager’s unhelpful friends. McKinsey & Co.'s weird interviews are coming soon to a bank near you
item.description:
When Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness fund got into trouble back in June, there were two things which saved him <https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-ipo-situational-awareness-leopold-aschenbrenner-2026-10> – his strong network of Silicon Valley friends and connections, many of them at Anthropic, and his incredibly valuable pre-IPO stake in Anthropic. (Well, maybe three things if you count Ken Griffin and Citadel, who took over Situational’s entire public equity portfolio and liquidated <https://www.reuters.com/markets/wealth/citadel-sheds-over-80-aggregate-risk-situational-awareness-portfolio-2026-08-21/> it quickly enough to avoid being caught by yesterday's Coreweave <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/14/coreweave-put-options-ai-trade.html> meltdown).
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
But 24-year-old Leopold's many friends, with whom he may once have attended Iliad wrestling parties, </news/ai-changing-quant-research-jobs> could be a lot less helpful soon. In fact, they could become unhelpful.
This is because, for Situational Awareness to realise the value in its Anthropic stake, Anthropic needs to IPO. When it does, it will be a publicly traded company. And when you own a big stake in a publicly traded company, the fact that you have so many close relationships with insiders starts to become a compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance> headache rather than an edge.
Aschenbrenner can hardly do anything to mitigate his insider status – his Silicon Valley network was the original “situation” which put him in a position where people handed over billions of dollars to a young person barely out of college who had been fired from two previous jobs. And so, compliance consultants like Greg Worsfold seem to think he will have to restrict his trading in Anthropic (and presumably other companies where he has close relationships). He might have to observe “blackout periods” around earnings releases and keep a paper trail showing that his investment theses were constructed based wholly on publicly available information.
Of course, this is potentially a problem for the future; Aschenbrenner might not want to sell his Anthropic stake this side of the Singularity. But it’s one that needs to be taken seriously. The last time we had a tech stock boom of any similar magnitude, there were plenty of people saying things like “no conflict, no interest” and it didn’t end up well for any of them.
Separately, role playing as an interview technique is rarely used in investment banking. </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> In other hiring contexts, it’s quite common for people to ask candidates to act out a scenario with their interviewer, to see how they would respond to a client. The advantage of doing this is that it allows an insight into someone’s personality and ability to think on their feet.
The disadvantage is that it is often really weird and embarrassing for the interviewer, so many bankers will flat out refuse to do it. (The only exception we’re aware of is David Bokman </news/2023/08/john-waldron-goldman-sachs>, the co-head of family office resources at Morgan Stanley, whose team uses roleplaying in order to see whether wannabe private bankers have the emotional intelligence to deal with the extremely rich).
But what if you could get an AI chatbot to take on the task? This is being trialled by McKinsey <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/mckinsey-interview-process-ai-7d08a69e?st=7LiQ2t&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink> & Co. From this autumn, entry-level candidates to the consulting firm will have a ten minute conversation with an “avatar” that has been trained to imitate stereotypical client personalities. Disappointingly, it doesn’t seem to have been given a cutsey name yet, but apparently it is not meant to provide “gotchas”. It is just meant to test candidates’ abilities to notice important information and to think rather than giving prepared answers.
It’s highly likely that this will soon be coming to banking interviews </news/70-top-banking-interview-questions-and-how-to-answer-them>too, and when it does it might be in a significantly more aggressive form. Sales and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>desks might be interested to find out how a candidate handles someone who is angry about a trading error, while capital markets teams might want to grade potential employees on their ability to tell a CEO that their IPO is pricing lower than expected.
What is less likely is any use of this sort of technology for anything other than entry-level roles and internships. </news/internship-investment-bank> As a way of quickly sorting through a large potential talent pool, the AI roleplay might be a very good way to structure the kind of interactions that make it easy to tell a potential future star from a dud. But there is a steep price in dignity and awkwardness. In the future, one way to measure the progress of your career will be by whether or not anyone would dare to ask you to do a role-playing exercise with an AI.
Meanwhile …
The $1.2bn fine which Bank of America got hit with seems to be quite disproportionate to any actual offences. The bank was fined for technical breaches relating to poorly designed alerting systems, but the penalty is larger than comparable cases in which large amounts of criminal money was provably laundered. It almost looks like a political vendetta by President Trump against Brian Moynihan. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-10-14/bank-of-america-took-a-1-2-billion-hit-for-the-wrong-reason>)
One of the things which senior investment bankers find almost as awkward as being asked to role-play at interviews is being asked to drum up clients for the wealth management side. Although “One Bank” sounds like a great slogan, it is just very difficult to switch between portraying oneself as a trusted advisor and trying to do a bit of cross-selling. Citi’s rainmakers are the latest to get the “just one client each” speech. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citi-wants-bankers-to-introduce-at-least-one-client-to-wealth-unit-by-end-of-2026-425cc201>)
Even with the benefit of the Situational Awareness trades, Citadel’s equities funds have been outperformed by its “tactical trading” (quant) unit. (Rupak Ghose <https://rupakghose.substack.com/p/the-year-of-the-systematic-hedge?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=1898843&post_id=220276728&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=k3np9&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email>)
The Perella Weinberg / Piper Sandler merger talks have ended. Apparently “a critical mass of Perella Weinberg’s top talent did not get on board with the deal” and the two boards couldn’t agree on “key financial and personnel matters”. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/dadac221-a4dd-4935-897e-7f7faebe8f17?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Antoine Iskander had been in talks with Millennium about spinning his pod out into an independent manager. Those might have been complicated by some losses this year, and now he’s going to go to Balyasny instead. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-14/millennium-trader-with-plans-to-spin-out-fund-to-join-balyasny?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261014&utm_campaign=author_19458291>)
It’s often a fun practical joke to drop a made-up name into conversation and see if the trading floor’s biggest blowhard claims to have worked with them or met them at an event. Apparently this works in tech too, where 53% of men surveyed claimed to have heard of AI pioneers “Craig Dalton” and “Susan Milner”, despite the fact they don’t exist. (WIRED <https://www.wired.com/story/men-cant-stop-faking-how-much-they-know-about-ai/>)

item.title: Balyasny hired the CIO of a quant fund with a sad past
item.description:
Balyasny Asset Management (BAM) has hired Limin Yang, a quant veteran who spent the past few years as chief investment officer at Nebula Research and Development, a New York-based stat arb fund.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Nebula was founded by Michael Graves, a former top quant portfolio manager at Cubist. Graves spent nine years at Cubist and resigned in 2018. He founded Nebula in 2019. Sadly, Graves reportedly died of a heart attack <https://www.businessinsider.com/paloma-redeems-money-quant-firm-nebula-following-michael-graves-death-2022-4>aged 49 while on vacation with his family three years later, leaving his wife to run the fund. Business Insider reported that Paloma Capital Partners, which had seeded Nebula, pulled money from the fund following Graves' sudden death.
Yang's LinkedIn profile says he acted as CIO at Nebula from August 2022, a few months after Graves' death, until September 2025. Yang has only just joined Balyasny, which declined to comment.
Prior to Nebula, Yang was an MD on the quant research team at BlackRock alternative asset management, a portfolio manager at Laurion Capital Management, and a prop trader at Credit Suisse.
