item.title: Hedge fund Point72 hired the former head of JPMorgan's equities central risk book
item.description:
The central risk book </news/2018/02/central-risk-desks-banking>of a bank can be one of the most powerful (and political) places to work outside of a trading desk. These teams monitor the trading strategies of various teams across their bank and can often deploy trading strategies </news/2018/07/central-risk-desks-are-getting-out-of-control>to hedge the risks those trading desks make. 'CRB' quants can be a natural fit for hedge funds; one of the former leaders of JPMorgan's equities CRB has just emerged at hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> Point72.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Ashot Ordukhanyan joined Point72 as head of risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank>technology, based in New York. He joined from risk intelligence fintech </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech> ActiveViam, where he was head of quant development for two years, but spent the two years before that as co-head of JPMorgan's equities CRB.
Ordukhanyan was also a top quantitative strategist </news/strats-jobs-investment-banks>(another kind of quant coveted by hedge funds </news/quant-strat-transition-to-hedge-fund-goldman-sachs>) across multiple banks. He spent 14 years at Goldman Sachs, rising from an associate to its co-head of US equity algorithmic trading strats. He left to run rates algorithmic trading at RBS before joining Deutsche Bank where he was Americas head of equity strats.
Risk teams in hedge funds can be very different to teams in banks. Giuseppe Paleologo, who worked in risk for both Citadel and Millennium, previously told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-06-21/giuseppe-paleologo-on-quant-investing-at-multi-strat-hedge-funds> that hedge fund risk staff manage pods like a trader would manage equities. Ordukhanyan appears to be tasked with building the systems that facilitate this.
The fund also lost one of its most senior technologists this month. Guillaume Gimonet, head of global treasury technology, left to become head of fixed income and ETF technology at Vanguard. He spent seven years at the fund and was previously head of macro risk and treasury technology. Gimonet was also previously an MD at Credit Suisse and CTO of George Soros' family office, Soros Fund Management.
Point72 declined to comment.

item.title: One of Citadel Securities' top London rates traders quietly vanished
item.description:
Citadel Securities has been growing its macro business, often with people it's hired from Goldman Sachs. As it does so, one of its long-serving London macro traders, who joined from Barclays in 2019, has gone.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
David Kwan, Citadel Securities' head of swaps trading in London, left the electronic trading firm at the end of July. We have not spoken to Kwan, and Citadel Securities declined to comment, but the FCA Register shows him leaving at the end of July.
Kwan is understood to have been a big deal </news/citadel-securities-keeps-ingesting-europe-s-top-rates-traders> during his time at Citadel Securities, but he was also low-key. It's not clear why he left. The firm has bolstered its macro team with a variety of big names like Nikhil Choraria, </news/nikhil-choraria> the former head of the European rates desk at Goldman Sachs, who has arrived this very month </news/london-s-inflation-traders-are-popular-on-the-recruiting-scene> and is based in London.
Kwan may have found a new role elsewhere. Or he may have retired following a longish career that began at Barclays in 2006. It's thought he's a fan of poker playing. We understand that Citadel Securities is moving US trader Jake Yudelowitz to London to become head of US treasury and swaps trading in the City. Yudelowitz joined Citadel Securities in 2020.
The changes at Citadel Securities' European rates business come as the firm has just published a document <https://www.citadelsecurities.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/CitadelSecurities_ResiliencyOfLiquidityProvisionInStressedMarkets_2026-FINAL.pdf> proclaiming the benefits it is bringing to fixed income markets "during periods of severe market stress."
The document says that contrary to claims by some trade organisations, new entrants to the market have been able to provide resilient liquidity in fixed income during market shocks, and that in doing so they've "compelled legacy intermediaries to up their game."

item.title: A lot of smaller banks can pay $1m+ in London too
item.description:
How much do top bankers earn in London? Whether you work for a big American bank </news/salaries-and-bonuses-goldman-sachs-jpmorgan-citi-baml-morgan-stanley> or a big European bank </news/barclays-hsbc-deutsche-bank-bnp-paribas-socgen-ubs-pay>, it is a lot. But what if you work for – hold your breath now here – a smaller bank?
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Well, the answer is still a lot. We looked at Pillar 3 disclosures from four banks that have a smaller European footprint than the usual JPMorgan- or Barclays-scale players: Jefferies, Wells Fargo, Mizuho, and Nomura.
The data mostly refers to salaries and bonuses for Material Risk Takers, or MRTs for short, defined as people whose “professional activities have a material impact on the risk profile of the firm,” per the UK’s FCA <https://www.handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/SYSC/19G/5.html#:~:text=A%20material%20risk%20taker%20is,assets%20that%20the%20firm%20manages.>.
Jefferies pay in London
Like the year before, Jefferies had the best paid MRTs in London across 2025. They earned over $1.7m on average in 2025 – but that was down significantly on what they made ($2m) in 2024.
This was primarily down to a decrease in salary, rather than bonus, although that decreased, too. Average salaries went from $1m to $814k between 2024 and 2025, while average bonuses went from $1m to $919k, on average. Jefferies have a 8x bonus cap </news/bonus-cap> implemented.
Wells Fargo pay in London
As in 2024, Wells Fargo had the worst-paid MRTs in London last year. But a hefty increase in both salary and bonus (up 22% and 39% on average) meant the discrepancy was less than before and that its MRTs averaged $1m in compensation, just a whisker behind Mizuho’s MRTs.
Wells Fargo offered the lowest salaries by some margin of the four banks we’ve compared here, just $450k on average, but sizeable bonuses: nearly $600k on average.
Mizuho pay in London
Mizuho paid its investment banking MRTs just $1.08m in 2025. A direct comparison to 2024 is not possible, as the firm did not disclose investment banking-specific compensation for that year.
Mizuho’s pay, despite being almost the same as Wells Fargo’s, was structured very differently. The firm paid average salaries almost $100k higher than Wells Fargo, and average bonuses almost $60k less.
Nomura pay in London
Investment banking MRT pay at Nomura increased between 2024 and 2025, going from $970k per head to $1.2m per head, overwhelmingly driven by an increase in average bonuses, which were up by 39%. The number of MRTs did decline, however, from 254 to 205.
Due to its number of MRTs, Nomura was the only bank that offered a breakdown of employees earning over €1m. While the total number of these earners increased by almost 13%, from 70 to 79, the vast majority were earning “just” €1m to €1.5m. The number earning over €1.5m actually decreased, from 34 to 32.

item.title: Morgan Stanley's ex-top strat seems to have left Rokos in London after a year
item.description:
Rokos Capital Management is moving some of its people to Athens with Chris Rokos, its founder. </news/chris-rokos-departing-hedge-fund-manager-is-not-just-a-330m-tax-payer>When it does, it seems that Yingyi Chu may not be with them.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Chu joined Rokos a year ago, in September 2025 and was the macro hedge fund's head of equity investment quants. The FCA Register shows him leaving the UK entity at the end of July.
Rokos declined to comment on Chu's whereabouts. Chu himself didn't respond to a request to comment. Sources suggest that he's left the firm. It's conceivable that he's simply moved to another of Rokos' current offices (New York, Abu Dhabi, Singapore).
Before Rokos, Chu spent 3.5 years at Capstone Investment Advisors. Before Capstone, he spent nearly five years at Morgan Stanley, where he was head of QIS strats. </news/strats-jobs-investment-banks> Before that he was a strat at Goldman.
If Chu has left Rokos, he may be going on to something similarly exciting. One headhunter observes that it is a fine launchpad for a career at other funds. We cannot say who might be leading the equity investment quants at Rokos instead.

item.title: Graduate salaries for accountants are 25+ years behind bankers
item.description:
Grant Thornton, the accounting firm </news/accounting-job-finance-banking>, is taking the fight to the Big Four </news/working-for-the-big-four-pwc-deloitte-ey-kpmg>. The Financial Times reported yesterday <https://www.ft.com/content/4d9eed56-c410-4e88-98a9-2420bedb5195?syn-25a6b1a6=1> that it intended to offer graduates in the UK £40k ($53k), more than the Big Four – who offer around £36k ($48k) – and much more than the £30k ($40k) that mid-tier firms offer.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
There is a slight embarrassment, however – it’s a rather paltry sum. The top investment banks in the UK have paid their graduates that for more than 20 years.
According to the AGR Graduate Recruitment Survey 2003, “the highest recorded starting salary was £40,000 for graduates at one of the leading international investment banks,” although it did not name the bank that offered said package. It is possibly Merrill Lynch, which the Guardian noted <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2000/sep/08/13> in September of the year 2000 to be offering yearly salaries of £37,500 to new graduates.
The Guardian’s September 2000 article also noted that, two years after graduation, a banker could earn more than £80k ($106k) a year working at a large international investment bank like UBS. That’s not too far off what a second-year analyst earns currently <https://www.canarywharfian.co.uk/investment-banking/634/investment-banking-salary-guide-2026-londoneurope> as a salary, although not when including bonuses.
Research from High Fliers <https://highfliers.co.uk/> shows that professional graduate salaries have increased between 70% to 135% since 2002. Both consulting and accounting graduate salaries have outgrown investment banking ones; 75% and 79% vs 71%, respectively.
There’s one place where accountants can compete with bankers, however: pay for senior professionals. A Big Four partner can easily earn over £1m ($1.3m) per year, which is broadly on par with what a senior investment banker earns – those employed by European banks </news/barclays-hsbc-deutsche-bank-bnp-paribas-socgen-ubs-pay>, at least. Senior bankers working for an American investment bank </news/salaries-and-bonuses-goldman-sachs-jpmorgan-citi-baml-morgan-stanley> can earn a bit more than that.

item.title: HSBC's Hong Kong bankers and the great perk withdrawal: "People had six children"
item.description:
As the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/37e6c9d9-2237-468d-b0c5-18b5d09c2ccc?syn-25a6b1a6=1>has reported, HSBC's Hong Kong bankers are adrift in a new reality. Once, they were the recipients of wildly generous perks. Now they're not. There are suggestions that HSBC might need to hike salaries as a result.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Until recently, the FT said HSBC offered its senior Hong Kong bankers both $38k school fee subsidies </news/george-saghir> per child and a generous allowance worth up to $25.5k to help them join private members clubs. Both have been discontinued, and starting from 2027 life assurance for future joiners will reportedly be less for existing staff.
The changes are part of an updated benefits framework for employees at HSBC and Hang Seng Bank that will begin in January. Most staff at the two banks will be unaffected. The big perks will only disappear at director level and above.
Reminiscing about the generous days past, one former HSBC managing director (MD) in Hong Kong, told us the higher perks were historically higher there to compensate for lower pay. "Salaries at HSBC were 10-15% lower than anywhere else, but they offered the best deal on club memberships in town," he said.
HSBC didn't comment on its historic pay. Last year, the bank paid its material risk takers - typically its most senior people - an average globally of $1.4m, </news/hsbc-is-paying-senior-bankers-who-stay-1-4m-and-senior-bankers-who-go-500k> putting it on a par with US banks. The pay differential may therefore have narrowed.
Existing employees at director level and above at HSBC in Hong Kong will continue to receive the US$38k school fee supplement, which will only be removed for new joiners from next year. This is fortunate as some Hong Kong bankers are understood to have had large families. "People had five or six children," said the ex-MD.
The removal of the US$25.5k club membership subsidy does not mean that HSBC's Hong Kong bankers will be meeting clients in Starbucks. The subsidy reportedly applied only to clubs that weren't whitelisted on HSBC's corporate membership list. This list is understood to include the likes of the Hong Kong Jockey Club and The American Club, so bankers will still be found in these hostelries.
It's not clear whether HSBC is also restricting access to the apartments it allegedly owns on the Peak and that are available as accommodation for very senior staff. The bank owns a mansion called Taipan House <https://finance.yahoo.com/news/iconic-taipan-house-eludes-executives-093000574.html>on the Peak. Until recently, this was occupied by Peter Wong, HSBC's chief executive for Asia, who retired in 2021. Last year, Wong was said <https://www.scmp.com/business/article/3315939/person-connected-hsbcs-wong-buys-luxury-flat-hong-kong-us159-million>to buy a US$16m apartment in Hong Kong's Southern District, so the mansion may now be available again.

item.title: Goldman Sachs' most junior bankers don't want to speak to you unless it's in person
item.description:
If you want to speak to a junior Goldman Sachs banker </news/goldman-sachs-internship-acceptance-rate>over the phone, there's a 99% chance they'd rather be doing something else. The bank recently released its annual summer analyst survey, which regularly asks Goldman Sachs </news/how-to-get-a-job-goldman-sachs> interns what their preferred method of communication is; for the fifth year running, phone calls ranked dead last by some distance.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Roughly 2,100 of Goldman's ~2500 summer analysts responded to the survey. In-person work was the most popular communication, preferred by 42% of interns, slightly down from 47% last year </news/goldman-sachs-summer-interns-email-phone-calls>. Interns said that working in the office was most important for mentoring and "forming spontaneous connections," but not as important for completing deliverables. The bank was one of the earliest to bring staff back into the office five days per week post-COVID. </news/2021/07/goldman-sachs-back-in-office>
The love for in-office work may also stem from a desire to be away from their screens. 34% of interns said they have more than 20 hours of screentime per week, with 7% having over 31 hours. 70% of interns said they use screen time limiting tools as well.
Despite this, text-based communications grew in popularity. Team chatrooms were second favourite for the second year running, however the gap between it and in-person communication fell from 12% to just 2%. Email's popularity more than doubled from 5% to 11%. The ability to check your responses with AI </news/ai-in-ma-banking>before sending them may have influenced this; outside of work, 19% said they use AI tools to verify facts and 36% said they use it to support their writing.

💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Roughly 2,100 of Goldman's ~2500 summer analysts responded to the survey. In-person work was the most popular communication, preferred by 42% of interns, slightly down from 47% last year </news/goldman-sachs-summer-interns-email-phone-calls>. Interns said that working in the office was most important for mentoring and "forming spontaneous connections," but not as important for completing deliverables. The bank was one of the earliest to bring staff back into the office five days per week post-COVID. </news/2021/07/goldman-sachs-back-in-office>
The love for in-office work may also stem from a desire to be away from their screens. 34% of interns said they have more than 20 hours of screentime per week, with 7% having over 31 hours. 70% of interns said they use screen time limiting tools as well.
Despite this, text-based communications grew in popularity. Team chatrooms were second favourite for the second year running, however the gap between it and in-person communication fell from 12% to just 2%. Email's popularity more than doubled from 5% to 11%. The ability to check your responses with AI </news/ai-in-ma-banking>before sending them may have influenced this; outside of work, 19% said they use AI tools to verify facts and 36% said they use it to support their writing.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Goldman Sachs’ nicest man seems to have won the prize. Millennium employees enter the Matrix
item.description:
In investment banking careers at the top level, perhaps the most important attribute to have is self-knowledge. If you underestimate your own capabilities, then you’ll be too timid, but if you overestimate your value to others, you might end up with a nasty surprise. John Waldron of Goldman Sachs is deservedly popular for being burdened with neither false modesty nor arrogance, and it seems that this may have put him into the lead in the board’s succession planning <https://www.wsj.com/finance/banking/goldmans-board-has-discussed-a-plan-to-name-john-waldron-as-its-next-ceo-7c5d90dd?mod=WSJ_home_feature_1_pos_3> for CEO David Solomon.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The firm has made it clear that the board talks about succession all the time, and that there is “no definitive timeline <https://www.ft.com/content/b8733b38-a94e-464e-9df7-dfcc757a58f0?syn-25a6b1a6=1>” for Solomon to step down (although 'executives close to Solomon' have reportedly <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-29/goldman-s-heir-apparent-faces-tough-task-keeping-deputies-happy?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260929&utm_campaign=author_21835441> been saying "no later than 2028."). Waldron has been the most likely candidate for a while now, ever since he was promoted to the board </news/john-waldron-goldman-sachs> eighteen months ago. He is thought to have the support of the partnership, and his appointment would be in line with one of the empirical regularities of bank CEOs – the “Principle of Flashy/Folksy Alternation </news/2023/05/andy-saperstein-ted-pick-morgan-stanley>”, which holds that an extrovert with star power (like David Solomon) will be succeeded by an archetypally nice, quietly spoken family man (like John Waldron).
Waldron once wanted to be a writer, </news/john-waldron> and like Marc Rowan </news/marc-rowan> at Apollo has been described as having a studious and academic air. However, although Waldron isn’t necessarily a big personality, he’s certainly not short of self confidence. Not so long ago </news/john-waldron-goldman-sachs>, he gave Goldman an ultimatum – he had a job offer from Apollo worth $500m. Money isn’t everything, but he was prepared to make the case to the board that if he was going to turn down life-transforming, generational wealth, it needed to be for something which gave him a reasonable degree of assurance that he could reach the top at GS.
This is a gutsy move. At any level of banking, it’s generally believed that you can get yourself “bid back” a maximum of once. Although the job is literally made of transactions, senior bankers don’t like to be put in a position of having to recognise that their relationships are transactional to a significant degree, and that if you want to retain the services of one of the world’s best bankers, you need to pay the going rate. Handling this kind of negotiation on behalf of Goldman Sachs was one of the skills which gained Waldron the nickname of “the banker whisperer”, so some people might have felt a little bit put out that he was capable of managing both sides of a tricky conversation.
And he may need to do a bit more whispering. Dan Dees and Ashok Varadhan, the co-heads of global banking and markets and asset management head Marc Nachmann, are all only a couple of years younger than Waldron, meaning that if he is indeed appointed, it’s likely that the next Goldman CEO will come from the following generation.
Elsewhere, all staff at Millennium Management are going to be given a “digital twin <https://www.businessinsider.com/millennium-employees-productivity-ai-digital-twin-2026-9>”, which sounds extremely futuristic. The reality seems to be a bit less science-fictional than the name, though – the digital twin is an AI agent, of course, but it’s main function seems to be “remembering their preferences and handling repetitive tasks, like research, meeting preparation, and inbox management.” Millennium are very keen to point out that the digital twins will not be given decision-making powers and certainly won’t be allowed to place trades; in all honesty, the combination of inbox, calendar and news feed sounds more like what used to be called a “home page” than anything else.
The digital twins are also meant to be proof against a kind of risk which many employees would fear, though – the possibility that their colleagues might like the robot better than the person who it’s meant to be a twin of. The digital twins are only allowed to correspond with their “owners”. Although the next project appears to be the creation of “digital teammates”, so Millennium analysts might still have reason to be at least a little bit worried.
Meanwhile …
Piper Sandler is, according to “a person familiar with the matter”, in talks to buy Perella Weinberg, creating a somewhat bigger super-boutique. The deal might close sectoral gaps in energy and consumer/retail. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-29/piper-sandler-in-talks-to-acquire-perella-weinberg-wsj-says>)
The Barclays return-to-office plan has been delayed somewhat – it was due to come in next Monday, but an email has gone out saying that “we are extending the implementation period” to 2027, “to ensure colleagues have the right support”. They are also apparently “reviewing our flexible working policy”. In general, it’s usually regarded as a bullish sign for the market <https://www.ft.com/content/3dad95df-0760-4c15-b9a2-c98b6ea1d1df> when employees get the upper hand on working conditions. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/5a1da44f-27c8-485c-a1ed-169a361d2b38>)
A somewhat less bullish sign is that bankers in the software sector are trying to handle private equity exits by recruiting small groups of investors rather than a public offer process, to avoid the risk of a high profile flop. (Pitchbook <https://pitchbook.com/news/articles/software-bankers-turn-to-back-room-negotiations-to-combat-market-jitters>)
Rama Variankaval is leaving JP Morgan after 23 years. His specialist advisory team working on low-carbon transition issues is going to be folded into a broader energy, geopolitical and environmental practice led by Heather Zichal, while former US NOAA chief scientist Sarah Kapnick will continue to run the climate advisory business. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-29/jpmorgan-global-head-of-corporate-advisory-exits-amid-reshuffle>)
The flow of JP Morgan dealmakers to Citi hasn’t completely stopped – Chris Power. JPM’s co-head of chemicals investment banking, is moving across to take the same role alongside Arkadi Nachimowski. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-hires-jpmorgans-powers-to-co-head-chemicals-after-shake-up-767ebad3?mod=topic_news>)
Proving once more that the tech sector have not learned much from the way that finance bros made themselves so unpopular, Instagram apparently made swag (in the form of “a/c priv” baseball caps, referring to attorney client privilege) for a team who were responsible for “tidying up” legal files ahead of litigation. (NY Post <https://nypost.com/2026/09/25/business/instagram-made-attorney-client-privilege-swag-hats-for-employees-who-concealed-kids-safety-docs-in-court-battle/>)
Follow me on X <https://x.com/MadameButcher>. Follow me on LinkedIn. <https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarahbutcherjournalist/>

item.title: How much experience do staff at electronic trading firms really have? Jane Street, HRT and more
item.description:
Quant trading firms </news/high-frequency-trading-hiring-and-pay> like Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street> have a reputation for hiring and developing young staff, </news/electronic-trading-summer-internship-pay>but the top firms have been doing that for decades. How much do the young guns actually dominate these trading firms today?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We've endeavoured to find out by analyzing the FINRA BrokerCheck profiles of personnel registered with the various entities of major electronic trading firms. We looked at 3,771 registered personnel across seven major firms, looking at how many years of financial services experience each company's employees have on average. This covers a range of functions, including securities traders, </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> operations professionals and client-facing roles. However, the data does not include most engineers, </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank>nor trading staff operating on venues not regulated by the SEC. People who joined from outside finance, or moved into US markets after years trading elsewhere, also only have a small slice of their experience counted.
With those caveats in mind, the average years of financial services experience across these firms was just 6.6 years. More than half of the registered personnel across these firms have less than five years of experience.
Jane Street, which had the most registered personnel of the seven firms, had the least experience on average of any US-native firm. Optiver and IMC staff had less experience on average, but are based in Amsterdam, which may be home to more of its senior staff. Jane Street had a greater proportion of staff with less than five years of experience than any US-based trading firm, and also the lowest proportion of staff with over 15 years of experience.
The most experienced firm was Susquehanna, where staff have 8.7 years of finance experience on average. The firm has the highest proportion of staff with over 15 years of experience. This makes sense, as it's the oldest US-native firm on the list; the firm was where most of Jane Street's founders worked before striking out on their own.
Over a quarter of registered personnel across these firms have just one year of experience in finance or less; at the Dutch firms, over 30% of registered staff are tadpoles. This could reflect the massive hiring sprees seen at these firms in recent years, or it could be a sign that most people leave before rising through the ranks.

item.title: Salaries and bonuses for top risktakers at Barclays, Deutsche Bank, UBS, and others
item.description:
Everyone knows that bankers make a lot of money. But just how much money do the most senior bankers in the industry – managing directors and heads of desks </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>– earn? As it turns out, a lot.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
The figures below were made public as part of the pay transparency requirements for various jurisdictions for 2025. The data mostly refers to salaries and bonuses for Material Risk Takers, or MRTs for short, defined as people whose “professional activities have a material impact on the risk profile of the firm,” per the UK’s FCA <https://www.handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/SYSC/19G/5.html#:~:text=A%20material%20risk%20taker%20is,assets%20that%20the%20firm%20manages.>, while UBS data refers to Key Risk Takers (KRTs), a self-created categorization. All data is derived from each bank's Pillar 3 or annual report remuneration disclosures.
The primary difference between MRTs and KRTs is that MRT designation requires an employee to earn £660k to be automatically considered one, while KRT designation is related to role. Previously, it automatically included those who earned over CHF2.5m or $2.5m, but that is no longer the case.
Where possible, we've broken out the data for MRTs in the investment banks only (labelled as 'investment banking MRTs' in the reports). These are front office MRTs only, working in areas like M&A </news/finance/get-a-job-in-ma> as well as capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> and sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>. The figures therefore don't include MRTs in control functions like risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank> and compliance </news/2022/07/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance> (for American banks’ control MRTs here </news/risk-compliance-pay-london>), or pay for members of management committees. For BNP Paribas, the data covers risk-takers related to the Corporate and Investment Bank (“CIB”), as opposed to “investment banking”. For UBS, it is for all KRTs across the bank.
The data shows that pay for MRTs and KRts was mixed compared to 2024. Average compensation rose at Barclays and HSBC, was flat at UBS, and fell at Deutsche, SocGen, and BNP. Barclays and UBS paid their MRTs/KRTs the most; SocGen paid its MRTs the least.
Salaries and bonuses at Barclays in 2025
Number of regulated staff: There were 812 investment bank MRTs at Barclays in 2025.
Average salary: The average Barclays investment bank MRT earned $862k in fixed compensation in 2025.
Average bonus: The average Barclays investment bank MRT earned $1.2m in variable compensation in 2025.
Average compensation: The average Barclays investment bank MRT earned $2.1m in total compensation in 2025.
Bonus breakdown: The average Barclays MRT (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) earned just 50% of their bonus in cash (60% deferred); 50% were in shares (69% deferred).
Deferred bonus: The average Barclays MRT’s (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) bonus was 65% deferred (46% cash, 54% shares).
Average severance payment: Barclays fired 32 MRTs (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) in 2025, who received $227k each in severance, on average.
Changes in compensation, 2024 vs 2025: The number of investment bank MRTs rose from 783 to 812, a 4% increase. Average salaries went from $909k per head to $862k per head, a 5% decrease. Average bonuses went from $1.1m per head to $1.2m per head, a 12% increase. Compensation as a whole therefore went from $2.0m to $2.1m, a 4% increase.
Distribution of staff earning over €1m:
Salaries and bonuses at HSBC in 2025
Number of regulated staff: There were 511 investment bank MRTs at HSBC in 2025.
Average salary: The average HSBC investment bank MRT earned $584k in fixed compensation in 2025.
Average bonus: The average HSBC investment bank MRT earned $819k in variable compensation in 2025.
Average compensation: The average HSBC investment bank MRT earned $1.4m in total compensation in 2025.
Bonus breakdown: The average HSBC MRT (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) earned just 52% of their bonus in cash (42% deferred); 48% were in shares (56% deferred).
Deferred bonus: The average HSBC MRT’s (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) bonus was 49% deferred (44% cash, 55% shares).
Average severance payment: HSBC fired 135 MRTs (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) in 2025, who received $504k each in severance, on average.
Changes in compensation, 2024 vs 2025: The number of investment bank MRTs fell from 535 to 511, a 4% decrease. Average salaries went from $611k per head to $584k per head, a 4% decrease. Average bonuses went from $738k per head to $819k per head, an 11% increase. Compensation as a whole therefore went from $1.35m to $1.40m, a 4% increase.
Distribution of staff earning over €1m:
Salaries and bonuses at Deutsche Bank in 2025
Number of regulated staff: There were 668 investment bank MRTs at Deutsche Bank in 2025.
Average salary: The average Deutsche Bank investment bank MRT earned $853k in fixed compensation in 2025.
Average bonus: The average Deutsche Bank investment bank MRT earned $1.1m in variable compensation in 2025.
Average compensation: The average Deutsche Bank investment bank MRT earned $1.9m in total compensation in 2025.
Bonus breakdown: The average Deutsche Bank MRT (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) earned just 50% of their bonus in cash (74% deferred); 50% were in shares (80% deferred).
Deferred bonus: The average Deutsche Bank MRT’s (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) bonus was 77% deferred (48% cash, 52% shares).
Average severance payment: Deutsche Bank fired 48 MRTs (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) in 2025, who received $494k each in severance, on average.
Changes in compensation, 2024 vs 2025: The number of investment bank MRTs rose from 609 to 668, a 10% increase. Average salaries went from $957k per head to $853k per head, an 11% decrease. Average bonuses went from $1.11m per head to $1.09m per head, a 2% decrease. Compensation as a whole therefore went from $2.1m to $1.9m, a 6% decrease.
Distribution of staff earning over €1m:
Salaries and bonuses at BNP Paribas in 2025
Number of regulated staff: There were 909 CIB MRTs at BNP in 2025.
Average salary: The average BNP CIB MRT earned $553k in fixed compensation in 2025.
Average bonus: The average BNP CIB MRT earned $772k in variable compensation in 2025.
Average compensation: The average BNP CIB MRT earned $1.3m in total compensation in 2025.
Bonus breakdown: The average BNP CIB MRT earned just 49% of their bonus in cash (53% deferred); 49% were in shares (54% deferred).
Deferred bonus: The average BNP CIB MRT’s bonus was 54% deferred (49% cash, 49% shares).
Average severance payment: BNP fired 39 MRTs (including, but not limited to, the CIB) in 2025, who received $473k each in severance, on average.
Changes in compensation, 2024 vs 2025: The number of CIB MRTs rose from 824 to 909, a 10% increase. Average salaries went from $576k per head to $553k per head, a 4% decrease. Average bonuses went from $781k per head to $772k per head, a 1% decrease. Compensation as a whole therefore went from $1.4m to $1.3m, a 2% decrease.
Distribution of staff earning over €1m:
Salaries and bonuses at Société Générale in 2025
Number of regulated staff: There were 384 investment bank MRTs at SocGen in 2025.
Average salary: The average SocGen investment bank MRT earned $496k in fixed compensation in 2025.
Average bonus: The average SocGen investment bank MRT earned $692k in variable compensation in 2025.
Average compensation: The average SocGen investment bank MRT earned $1.2m in total compensation in 2025.
Bonus breakdown: The average SocGen investment bank MRT earned just 50% of their bonus in cash (57% deferred); 50% were in shares (57% deferred).
Deferred bonus: The average SocGen investment bank MRT’s bonus was 57% deferred (50% cash, 50% shares).
Average severance payment: SocGen fired 10 MRTs (including, but not limited to, the investment bank) in 2025, who received $983k each in severance, on average.
Changes in compensation, 2024 vs 2025: The number of investment bank MRTs rose from 347 to 384, an 11% increase. Average salaries went from $518k per head to $496k per head, a 4% decrease. Average bonuses went from $711k per head to $692k per head, a 3% decrease. Compensation as a whole therefore went from $1.23m to $1.19m, a 3% decrease.
Distribution of staff earning over €1m:
Salaries and bonuses at UBS in 2025
Number of regulated staff: There were 755 KRTs at UBS in 2025.
Average salary: The average UBS KRT earned $646k in fixed compensation in 2025.
Average bonus: The average UBS KRT earned $1.4m in variable compensation in 2025.
Average compensation: The average UBS KRT earned $2.1m in total compensation in 2025.
Bonus breakdown: The average UBS KRT earned just 43% of their bonus in cash (none deferred); 57% were in shares (100% deferred).
Deferred bonus: The average UBS KRT’s bonus was 57% deferred (100% shares).
Changes in compensation, 2024 vs 2025: The number of KRTs fell from 835 to 755, a 10% decrease. Average salaries went from $659k per head to $646k per head, a 2% decrease. Average bonuses went from $1.38m per head to $1.41m per head, a 2% increase. Compensation as a whole therefore went from $2.0m to $2.1m, a 1% increase.

item.title: Jump Trading joined the $1m per head club in London as average pay rose 55% in 2025
item.description:
2025 was a great year for both electronic trading firms </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> and the staff that work in them. Pay for the top firms in London </news/hft-pay-london> has always been high, but multiple firms paid out average packages of $1m (£756k) last year. They include Jane Street, </news/jane-street-pay> Hudson River Trading </news/hudson-river-trading-pay-uk-high-frequency-trading>... and also Jump Trading.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Accounts for 'Jump Trading International Limited' released today on the UK's Companies House. They showed that overall headcount rose by 36 to a total of 336 employees. The headcount rise was split almost evenly between the front and back office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>, with the latter growing slightly more. At the same time, average 'salaries and wages' per head rose to $1.07m (£809k), up from $687k the year before. It's the highest average pay recorded at Jump Trading International (excluding director pay) for the decade so far.
Jump made some senior hires last year in London. In the front office, it hired Mariano Arrieta, a former portfolio manager at both Balyasny </news/balyasny-asset-management-paid-its-average-uk-portfolio-manager-1-8m-last-year-but-do-not-be-deceived> and Millennium, </news/millennium-hired-a-senior-portfolio-manager-from-schonfeld-in-hong-kong> who joined in August as a quant trader. In the back office, it hired Loren Puchella Fiore </news/jane-street-python-machine-learning-loren-fiore-jump-trading>, who was Jane Street's Asia head of machine learning for over six years. Today, Jump has 14 openings available in London with a particular focus on high-performance computing systems.

item.title: Millennium hired a senior portfolio manager from Schonfeld in Hong Kong
item.description:
Becoming a senior portfolio manager at Millennium </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium>isn't easy. The hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> interviews 3,000 people per year and hires a small fraction of them for those roles. It helps to be coveted by rival hedge funds; Alexandre Yun, Millennium's latest hire in Hong Kong, was hired by two rival multistrats in the last four years before joining.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Yun joined as a senior PM focused on long/short equity strategies for global technology stocks. He previously spent two and a half years at Schonfeld </news/adam-grunfeld-schonfeld-millennium>as a PM operating the same kind of strategy, but most recently was sitting out a six month period of gardening leave. Yun also spent a brief 5 months at Balyasny, </news/dmitry-balyasny-hedge-fund> again focused on long/short equities; his six month garden leave period after leaving was longer than the time he spent actually working at the firm.
Yun seems to be playing the field after getting out of a long term professional relationship. He spent 16 years and was a partner at Cavalry Asset Management, the hedge fund of John Hurley, who has since left to become an ambassador for the US government.
More senior PMs may soon follow. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-25/millennium-s-new-cash-raise-draws-30-billion-in-client-demand> reported last week that Millennium is set to close on $22bn of new commitments as part of its latest capital raise.

item.title: Morning Coffee: The heroic age of investment banking is coming to an end. HSBC hasn’t cut as many top bankers as you think
item.description:
Although “Industry” is the HBO series most directly relevant to the lives of young investment bankers, as your career progresses, you might learn more lessons by rewatching “Game of Thrones”. In particular, the way that the fantasy epic demonstrates and reinforces the message that neither success in battle nor the ability to form relationships with dragons are particularly well correlated to administrative ability in a large organisation.
For most of the history of financial services, the great franchises have risen and fallen to the recurring refrain of “our best banker just became our worst manager”. But is this era coming to an end? Looking at Blackstone <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-26/blackstone-cements-shift-from-star-dealmakers-with-baratta-exit>, it seems that it might.
With the retirement of Joe Baratta, Blackstone’s head of private equity, the company has confirmed that there will be no single executive replacing him, and the only executives left on the board will be founder/CEO Steve Schwarzmann and President/COO Jon Gray. Managing the company, and making morale-boosting videos </news/jon-gray-blackstone>, is now more important than being a rainmaker oneself.
Of course, Gray was a dealmaker not so long ago. The leveraged buyout of Hilton Hotels which he led is still regarded as being one of the most profitable private equity transactions in history. And Schwarzmann was only in a position to found a company like Blackstone because he’d had so much success doing deals in his banking career.
So it’s not so much that the investment banking industry is ever likely to draw its leadership from anywhere other than its own most successful bankers. It’s more that the days are over when people like John Mack </news/2022/11/ageing-bankers> or John Gutfreund <https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/10/business/dealbook/john-gutfreund-who-ran-salomon-brothers-at-its-apex-is-dead-at-86.html> were able to run the largest banks on the Street while also continuing to maintain their personal franchise. This is just about possible at a boutique, but in a larger investment bank, there are two fatal flaws with the “player-manager” model.
One is that although making transactions happen is the most difficult thing in banking, it’s not the only thing. Cost control and risk management matter too, and it’s not fair to the rest of the business to have someone in charge of these important functions when their head and heart are still on the front line.
And the other is that when the boss has a big personal franchise, it’s hard to tell anyone else that they ought to put the team before themselves. This isn’t just a problem for bankers; law firms <https://www.ft.com/content/ba19ec85-c736-4cfd-9a85-4e1ddf1938e5?syn-25a6b1a6=1> always have problems negotiating the tricky balance between incentivising their partners, and building a business rather than a group of private practices which happen to share a roof.
The heroic age is not completely over - Rich Handler at Jefferies, for example, still deals personally with a lot of clients. And nearly every Wall Street CEO takes pride in being able to contribute to winning big transactions. But with every generational change of leadership, the importance of general managerial skills seems to grow, and the importance of big personal revenue production shrinks.
Elsewhere, one of the statistics which people used to understand the scale of the cost-cutting program launched by Georges Elhedery was the sharp decline in the number of “material risk takers” identified in regulatory disclosures. But according to Pam Kaur <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hsbcs-outgoing-cfo-pam-kaur-senior-bankers-have-not-been-shown-the-door-53f03dac>, the chief financial officer, this might have been a slightly misleading metric.
She says that “Every year we go back and take a look at the definition of a material risk taker. Some people cease to be MRTs because we have reworked that definition… you can have a rule that says that if you are sitting in certain meetings, by definition you are a material risk taker. That is what we have reworked”.
It’s certainly true that the MRT definition is flexible, and has always been subject to a certain degree of grade inflation. Bankers may have insisted on being designated as one simply because it used to be correlated with perceived importance, and with a high level of compensation. HSBC has made severance payments to quite a few highly paid bankers, but it seems that in many cases, it might have been more of a matter of telling them to get real.
Meanwhile…
Jefferies gave some reason for optimism about Q3 results, as its trading and banking revenues were both up double-digit amounts on last year. (Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/jefferies-quarterly-profit-jumps-deal-surge-equities-trading-strength-2026-09-28/>)
A slightly unusual move from buy side to sell side, as Bennett Schachter goes from Elliott Management to lead the capital advisory practice at Centerview. He was previously a SPAC specialist at Morgan Stanley. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-28/centerview-hires-elliott-s-capital-markets-specialist-schachter>)
Graticule Asset Management Asia lost most of its AuM in 2023, when it was caught on the wrong side of short term interest rates during the Silicon Valley Bank collapse. But it’s now built its way back to $3bn under management, through a combination of separately managed accounts, use of AI agents to keep costs down and, presumably, very tactful conversations with clients. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/adam-levinson-back-svb-collapse-forced-graticule-hedge-fund-close-2026-9>)
Goldman Sachs is introducing measures to make it easier for individual shareholders to vote their shares, to dilute the effect of activists objecting to the remuneration votes. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-28/goldman-revamps-shareholder-voting-options-after-fight-over-pay?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260928&utm_campaign=author_21835441>)
If you think that banking titles are confusing, try law. Kirkland & Ellis have “salaried partners”, “equity partners” and now “senior income partners”. Some of these titles are highly competitive and sought after while others are “glorified twelfth year associates”. It must be hard to work in an “up or out” culture when people aren’t even really sure what constitutes a promotion. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/kirkland-elliss-up-or-out-culture-is-getting-more-complicated-9c062f2b?mod=homepage>)
Do you think you can predict what the 2030s equivalent of the Patagonia fleece vest will be? Jane Street is advertising for a “swag program manager” who not only has to have seven years of experience in putting logos on things, but needs to be “comfortable building models and forecasts”. The right person could earn up to $200,000 and will have the chance to create knickknacks and tchotchkes that today’s traders can only dream of. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jane-street-quant-six-figures-swag-manager-2026-9>)

item.title: Millennium & Point72 adding data centre expertise amidst questions over hedge funds' strategies
item.description:
If you're a big multistrategy hedge fund </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-hiring> using AI to generate alpha, or an electronic trading firm </news/difference-between-electronic-trading-firms> using AI to make markets and hedge trades, do you really need your own data centre? What if you just....rent space in one?
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
With data centre capital expenditure expected to hit at least $800bn <https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2026/global-investment-in-ai-infrastructure.html#:~:text=On%20an%20annual%20basis%2C%20data,trillion%20per%20year%20in%202050.>this year, different strategies are emerging with regards to data centre provisions. Some firms, like Jump Trading, QRT, XTX and Jane Street </news/jane-street-data-centre>have data centres for their own use. Jump, for example, says it has three "large purpose built" research data centres. A data centre is being built for Qube in Iceland. <https://hedgeweek.com/news/qrt-goes-to-iceland-in-search-of-market-edge>XTX is building a data centre in Kajaani, Finland. Jane Street was reported <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-04/jane-street-plans-new-data-center-as-compute-power-runs-scarce> to be in the early stages of building and financing its own data centre in June.
Less clear are the data centre strategies of major hedge funds. Millennium and Citadel declined to comment for this article and Point72 and DE Shaw didn't respond to a request to comment. But data centres are clearly on the agenda.
Earlier this year, for example, Millennium added Joseph Lenox from Citadel as its global head of data centres and Christian Blanc </news/hedge-fund-millennium-hired-a-goldman-sachs-md-to-expand-its-data-centres-team> from Goldman Sachs as his apparent deputy. In London, it's just hired David Rosa Casado from Deutsche Bank as a network automation lead, focused on AI engineering. Similarly, Point72 hired Peter Deignan from Morgan Stanley as a data centre programme manager in January. Balyasny has had a global head of data centre management since last August, in the form of Kevin Monahan, who arrived from CBRE.
Where are these data centres? In current job ads, Millennium says it has two data centres in New Jersey. The location of other funds' data centres is less clear. There are suggestions that because major firms have investments in data centre providers like CoreWeave (Citadel, Jane Street </news/jane-street-compute>), Nscale (Citadel, Jane Street, Point72) and because Point72's Turion fund is focused on data centres and AI investments, they may be able to secure preferential access to facilities and don't need their own sites. This has not been confirmed.
There are suggestions, too, that because firms like Citadel and Citadel Securities are partnered with Google Cloud, <https://cloud.google.com/transform/citadel-securities-reimagine-quantitative-reseach-cloud-scale-speed>they don't need data centres of their own. Neither firm is believed currently to have its own data centre for this reason.
Running your own data centre requires talent. Jump Trading, for example, has hired three data centre engineers in the past month (Adam Motto from StoneX in New York, James Diley from Oracle in Texas, and Lalit Gangurde from Amazon in Mumbai). Jump is also advertising multiple data centre roles, including a data infrastructure planning lead.
Data centre jobs are fundamentally about real estate, which is presumably why Hadrien Karabachian, a vice president in BlackRock's real estate division recently became chief of staff at data centre provider Data4 in Paris.
Karabachian didn't respond to a request to comment for this article, but one industry insider suggested the physical nature of data centres is problematic for multistrategy hedge funds which are usually run on comparatively short time horizons.
Constructing a data centre requires a long-term commitment. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-13/jane-street-lease-backs-2-25-billion-of-green-data-center-bonds>reported in August, for example, that Jane Street had entered a 15-year lease on a data centre in Oklahoma.
Speaking off the record, one senior technologist with a history of working across the quant hedge fund industry, suggested these time horizons can be difficult for some multistrategy firms to handle.
"A pod shop pays its portfolio managers based on their own P&L after expenses and recovers its costs through the pass-through structure </news/hedge-fund-pass-throughs>," he said. "But what happens when you realise you can't get the compute you want from AWS and so you have to build a data centre of your own. - How do you charge that forward cost to a pod when those PMs might not even be there to benefit?"

item.title: 22-year-old Goldman alum at Kalshi branded "the coffee boy" by gaming exec feuding with the CEO
item.description:
Working at a startup </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech> like Kalshi </news/prediction-markets-jobs-kalshi-polymarket> instead of a bank has its perks and drawbacks. You can get into high-impact client-facing roles much more quickly than a banking analyst, but you can also be subject to the bizarre sequence of events recently faced by Nicolas Hull. He joined Kalshi's business development team as a graduate this year after internships at Goldman </news/goldman-sachs-internship-acceptance-rate> and two private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> firms, but was publicly mocked on X <https://x.com/VictorRocha1/status/2104094625644548265?s=20> over the weekend by Victor Rocha, conference chair of the Indian Gaming Association.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Rocha said that Kalshi had been emailing tribal leaders to organize meetings at the Global Gaming Expo conference in Las Vegas, and that Hull would be the one conducting those meetings. "They're sending the coffee boy," Rocha said, describing him as "the intern... I think this might be his first big boy job." Rocha also mocked the appearance <https://x.com/VictorRocha1/status/2104363904742957485?s=20>of another Kalshi employee that replied to the tweet and replied "f*** off" <https://x.com/VictorRocha1/status/2104287262293000330?s=20> to Max Crowley, Kalshi's VP of business development, who defended Hull and said that the firm had already reached an agreement with one tribal leader with "more on the way." Rocha, Hull and Kalshi each did not respond to a request for comment.
This is part of an ongoing feud between the Indian Gaming Association and Kalshi. The New York Post <https://nypost.com/2026/09/25/business/inside-kalshi-ceo-tarek-mansours-testy-relationship-with-indian-casinos-and-how-it-could-pose-an-existential-threat-lying-little-twerp/> reported last week that Kalshi tried to hire Rocha as an advisor last year, but that talks fell through after some ill-fated meetings in which Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour allegedly tried to discuss their shared "generational burden." <https://nypost.com/2026/09/25/business/inside-kalshi-ceo-tarek-mansours-testy-relationship-with-indian-casinos-and-how-it-could-pose-an-existential-threat-lying-little-twerp/#:~:text=Mansour%2C%20in%20turn,a%20Syrian%20occupation>Rocha subsequently described Mansour as a "lying little twerp," and said that his company should be "curb stomp[ed]."
Much of the feud hinges on the notion that Kalshi says its event contracts are financial instruments, which are not subject to gambling regulations. Kalshi markets these contracts as an opportunity to bet on events without going up against a house.

item.title: Ex-UBS technology MDs are resurfacing in fine jobs elsewhere
item.description:
As the fourth quarter approaches, UBS is widely expected to cut some more costs. </news/ubs-cuts-hiring> If it does, technologists may yet be targeted following the recent departure of Michael Farthing, </news/three-equities-m-ds-are-leaving-ubs-in-london-one-is-leaving-for-a-new-role> the Swiss bank's head of global markets execution technology. It's cheering, then, that some of UBS's ex-technologists have quietly been arriving in very big jobs elsewhere.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Most impressively, Lawrence Booker, who was a former managing director in AI, data and analytics at UBS, before leaving in the wake of the Credit Suisse acquisition in 2023, resurfaced at Goldman Sachs six months ago.
Booker didn't respond to a request to comment for this article, but after nearly 19 years at UBS in London, a year out focused on Brazilian jiu-jitsu and a brief spell as a director of an AI solutions provider, he's now a managing director at Goldman Sachs in London, where he's helping to roll out AI for Goldman's sales team.
In this role, Booker appears to be working with Chris Churchman, the Goldman Sachs partner and head of Marquee who also formerly worked for UBS. Churchman joined Goldman in 2021 after running FX trading for UBS in the Americas. He's now chair of the global banking and markets AI working group.
It's not clear what Farthing intends to do next. He and other UBS technologists could conceivably hit up their former colleagues at Goldman Sachs. Alternatively, Mike Dargan </news/mike-dargan-ubs>, the former group chief information officer at the Swiss bank, is now chief executive of German fintech N26.
UBS declined to comment for this article. One senior technologist there said life there was highly pressured in the technology team since the merger and that the "brutal" integration of Credit Suisse was combined with an aggressive migration to the cloud.

item.title: Vanguard pay in the UK: $830k+ for your boss, $160k for you
item.description:
Vanguard is one of the more interesting asset management </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-asset-management> firms in the world. Owned by its own funds, it is famously lean, offering mainly minimalist, passive index funds to its mainly retail customer base. Despite that, it has almost as many employees as rival Blackrock – and a startling pay disparity.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
2025 Regulatory filings from Vanguard Asset Management, Ltd <https://fund-docs.vanguard.com/MIFIDPRUPublicDisclosure.pdf> – the firm’s main UK subsidiary – shed some light on who exactly is earning what. In short: the firm’s leadership is making great money. Everyone else, however, is lagging.
Average pay in 2025 at Vanguard Asset Management Ltd. (VAM) was £137k ($182k). Around two-thirds of that – £93k ($123k) – came from salaries, and a third – £44k ($58k) – came from bonuses. But beneath those numbers was a significant disparity.
VAM’s 17 members of senior management earned salaries of approximately £232k ($308k) and bonuses of £448k ($594k) on average that same year. Total compensation for this small group was therefore £680k ($902k), on average, in 2025.
Pay for the firm’s 14 non-management MRTs wasn’t far behind. MRTs are a regulatory invention that refer to people whose “professional activities have a material impact on the risk profile of the firm,” per the UK’s FCA <https://www.handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/SYSC/19G/5.html#:~:text=A%20material%20risk%20taker%20is,assets%20that%20the%20firm%20manages.>. VAM MRTs earned salaries of £237k ($314k) and bonuses of £390k ($517k) on average in 2025, for total compensation of £627k ($832k).
Things were not so good for the remaining 1,085 VAM employees who were neither senior managers nor MRTs. These people, who represented 97% of the firm's UK workforce, earned average salaries of just £89k ($118k) and average bonuses of just £33k ($44k), for total compensation of just £122k ($160k), on average in 2025.
It’s a significant disparity. For comparison, the average employee at Goldman Sachs International, the US bank’s UK subsidiary, earned $963k </news/london-goldman-sachs> (£726k) after a strong 2025, which was around 57% of what the firm’s MRTs earned </news/salaries-and-bonuses-goldman-sachs-jpmorgan-citi-baml-morgan-stanley> in the UK in that same year. At VAM, the equivalent figure is just 21%.
Vanguard had a pretty successful 2025 in the UK, according to recently-released figures from Vanguard Asset Services, a subsidiary of the firm, on companies house. Its UK-domiciled assets under management (AuM) was £106bn ($141bn) at the end of the year, up from £88bn ($117bn) at the start, an increase of around 20%. Revenue was up less dramatically, by just 6%, but profit was up more significantly, by around 32%.

item.title: Morgan Stanley went on a summer hiring spree for its European credit trading team
item.description:
Summer is over and Morgan Stanley's London credit trading team seems plumper than it was previously.
The US bank is understood to have added at least seven people to its European credit team since July, many in the mid-ranks.
The new recruits include Jessie Murrall, a former vice president (VP) at RBC Capital Markets in London, who's joined the European investment grade business led by Elizabeth Jeong. They also include Nick Scott, an executive director in credit sales who began his career at Morgan Stanley as an associate in leveraged credit trading, and who's returned after a 17 year hiatus at the bank. Scott was most recently at Aurel BGC.
The other summer recruits included Jonathan Soares from Citi, Rishad Ahmed from Enzo Asset Management, Marina Alvarez from JPMorgan, Roko Markesic from DWS and Andre Zucher from MFS Investment Management. Alvarez is in sales.
Alongside the hires, Morgan Stanley has also shuffled people internally. Annamaria Palmieri moved into European CDS trading in August after working in Morgan Stanley's equity derivatives business. Yiyi Dong in high yield and investment grade analytics was appointed to lead high yield credit trading in Europe.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Morgan Stanley declined to comment on the changes. The US bank's global credit business is run by Rehan Latif, who joined the bank 22 years ago.
Under Latif, Morgan Stanley has been creating an integrated credit trading platform and investing in technology and infrastructure and people after taking an early view that the market was heading for increased electronification. This has coincided with various senior departures </news/morgan-stanley-credit-traders-leaving> in recent years. However, there have also been significant arrivals, including that of Pauline Doutriaux from SocGen in 2022. Doutriaux is thought to have helped develop the bank's new algorithmically-integrated model in which traders, quants and technologists work together.
While there have been summer arrivals, there have also been summer exits. Jon Stead </news/hedge-fund-jain-global-hired-morgan-stanley-s-head-of-high-yield-trading-in-london>, Morgan Stanley's head of high yield trading, trod the path to Jain Global in August. Diego Grandi, a VP in leveraged loan trading, went to King Street in September.

item.title: Stripe's top engineers are producing 10x as much as they did in 2024
item.description:
The term '10x engineer' is an overused cliche in the world of tech startups and scaleups, but thanks to AI tools, they might become a lot more common. In a video released by Anthropic <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_lzYIvtEaQ>last week, Stripe </news/stripe-has-put-an-ex-hsbc-compliance-guy-in-charge-of-its-uk-office> CEO Patrick Collison revealed that some engineers at Stripe are producing literally ten times as much as the average engineer was producing a few years ago.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"I was speaking with one engineer at Stripe this morning, and over the course of H1 he had more than 600 pull requests [changes to a codebase] merged," Collison said. "Every one of them was written with AI." This equates to 23 'PRs' per week. In 2024, </news/stripe-high-performance-engineers>Stripe made a total of 1,145 pull requests per day, equivalent to 2.3 per developer per week.
Stripe's AI usage has had a tangible impact on hiring. Collison said that the fintech has seen "at least 6x speed up" on certain projects; managers used to ask for additional staff when completing a project but can now do it three times as fast with half the amount of people using agents. Despite smaller teams, Collison said that "quality per pull request over the last 18 months has gone up" too.
Stripe said in a blog post <https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2>earlier this year that it merges 1,300 PRs per week which are written entirely by 'Minions', the firm's in-house agentic coding tools. It's not clear what proportion of total PRs are done agentically; during this year's Stripe Sessions, <https://stripe.com/gb/sessions/2026/opening-remarks-and-product> Collison said that, in 2025, the fintech produced "well over a thousand production pull requests per day," suggesting that at least three fifths of PRs at Stripe still have human involvement.
Implementing AI has not been faultless. Collison said that "incidents per unit time" was also up, but that those incidents were "very minor" and that the firm's prior investment into reliability infrastructure has meant that "total reliability is essentially unchanged." Stripe said in 2024 that it checks each change to the codebase over one million times, and makes a total of over "six billion test runs each day." </news/stripe-code-culture> Collison said Stripe has also been implementing guardrails around sensitive data since 2017 which "kind of accidentally put us in a better position when agentic development came along."

item.title: A top French M&A banker left HSBC. Now he has one of the biggest jobs in France
item.description:
Being a top tier M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> banker is a lot like being a top footballer. Take Thierry Henry, for example, who had a stellar junior career, a rather lacklustre stint in Italy, and then got himself back to the top in his record-setting time at Arsenal. Some M&A careers are not so different.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Alexandre Courbon joined BNP this month as co-head of its French advisory business. Courbon was off the market since March, and he was last head of European M&A at HSBC, a firm he was with since 2019 – and doomed since last year, when HSBC announced that it was closing its entire M&A franchise outside of Asia. BNP declined to comment, and Courbon did not respond to a request for comment.
It’s a pretty stellar step up for Courbon, all things considered. Data from market intelligence firm LSEG placed BNP as the 4th biggest M&A player in France across 2025, with around $37bn in deal volume closed. HSBC, by contrast, was 18th, with just $5bn in deal volume closed. In fact, LSEG’s figures suggest that BNP’s French M&A activity alone was on par with HSBC’s entire EMEA M&A footprint.
Much like Henry, Courbon has had an interesting career trajectory. Originally a lawyer with white shoe firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton, he moved over to Societe Generale in Paris to work in its industrials M&A team. Just eight years later, he was appointed head of SocGen’s French M&A team and made an MD in the process. He spent four years there before moving on to HSBC.

item.title: Morning Coffee: What it's like when Citadel really wants you. Another JPMorgan expenses case
item.description:
It's not easy to get a job at hedge fund Citadel. If you apply out of university, you will be up against thousands of other people and there will be an acceptance rate of 0.5% </news/hedge-funds-are-cool-again-for-graduates-big-tech-is-out> or less. If you apply for a more senior role you might encounter the ghSMART </news/2023/04/ghsmart-interview>five hour interview scrutinising your childhood.
If Citadel wants you, though, it will accommodate you. It has accommodated Alexey Poyarkov, </news/tgs-to-citadel> whom - as we were first to report last week - it has hired from super-secretive, super-old school, quant trading firm TGS </news/tgs-management-company-llc> Management Company LLC.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
TGS is based in Irvine, which is in Orange County, California. Having extracted Poyarkov from the firm, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-25/citadel-hunts-for-managers-of-machines-in-quant-hiring-push> reports that Citadel will have an office in Irvine too. Citadel's own site <https://www.citadel.com/what-we-do/global-quantitative-strategies/> says that Poyarkov will be leading a new business called GQS SCI, based in Irvine. But Citadel's own map of current office locations <https://www.citadel.com/who-we-are/office-locations/> shows no office in Irvine. Nor does its most recent ADV form. Poyarkov will seemingly be the start of his very own office.
Citadel didn't respond to a query on whether this is the case. Unlike rival fund Millennium </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium>, which has a multitude of small offices accommodating the needs of experienced portfolio managers, Citadel has historically tended to cluster its employees in a few places (New York, Miami, once upon a time, Chicago). A new office in Orange County looks like a departure from this trend. Citadel also likes to have people actually in its offices, so Poyarkov is unlikely to be working from his garden shed.
There are two reasons why Citadel would have opened a new Irvine office for Poyarkov. One is that he is so very talented that Citadel would have done anything to hire him. This is possible: as Citadel itself notes, Poyarkov is a "two-time math Olympiad gold medallist. </news/citadel-olympiad>" When TGS hired Poyarkov in 2016, the Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-quants-run-wall-street-now-1495389108> reported that he was subject to a bidding war and that despite the fact that he had no previous finance experience, he was told he could earn $700k in his first year there. Ten years later, Poyarkov is presumably able to name his price, and his location.
The second reason Citadel would have opened an office in Irvine is that Irvine is where TGS's other people are based. Bloomberg says Poyarkov will be expanding Citadel's quantitative investment organisation and running a new team based on systematic trading of global equities. This team will be hiring people from AI labs. Maybe it will be hiring other people from TGS too?
Separately, a few months ago there was a FINRA arbitration in which a JPMorgan broker (Brent Ryan Bodner </news/perella-weinberg-partners-cut>) spent $642 on a deli platter to share with a client and was fired because JPMorgan thought he was eating the platter himself. Bodner contested this and was awarded $4.2m in damages.
Now another JPMorgan employee claims that he has been targeted as the result of an expenses case. In court filings, Brian Larson, a senior associate at the bank in the US, reportedly says <https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/jpmorgan-chase-lgbtq-discrimination-lawsuit-b3055842.html>JPMorgan queried his expenses of $40 for two Uber rides and that he was subsequently let go even though his JPMorgan manager had approved the expenses.
Larson's Uber rides were to Pride events, which he says he was attending with JPMorgan's approval. Now he's suing JPMorgan and claiming he was discriminated against on the grounds of his sexual orientation. JPMorgan says it conducted a "thorough internal investigation we found no evidence to substantiate Mr. Larson’s claims.” Larson was on a short-term programme which didn't guarantee a full-time role, said the bank.
A source at the bank told the Independent there were "gaps" in Larson's performance. Nonetheless, expenses claims at JPMorgan appear to be a risky business.
Meanwhile...
Citadel re-recruited Matt Giannini to hire people for its equities business. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/citadel-hires-matt-giannini-business-development-walleye-hedge-fund-talent-2026-9>
“We've seen growing interest from large marketmakers and hedge funds to recycle risks from autocallable issuers. That was practically non-existent two years ago and it’s now helping free capacity on the dealer side and allow the overall supply of structured products to grow.” Citadel Securities, Jane Street, Millennium Management and Optiver have moved into this business. (IFR) <https://www.ifre.com/topic-codes/2490111/risk-recycling-revolution-fuels-banks-structured-products-boom>
People are starting to wonder about AI-related IPOs. SB Energy and Nscale, two data centre builders preparing for initial public offerings in New York are pursuing valuations of $50bn and $35bn respectively. But they have revenues of less than $140m. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/b5707707-730e-40d3-9ff7-8ebfe27d5708?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
At least 10 senior bankers at ANZ Group Holdings are leaving the firm by October as Nuno Matos continues to overhaul the business. (Straits Times) <https://www.straitstimes.com/business/at-least-10-anz-senior-bankers-in-hong-kong-singapore-and-australia-to-exit-in-revamp>
Polymarket allows you to bet on whether banks like JPMorgan will fail. The FDIC isn't sure about this. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-25/polymarket-wagers-on-bank-failures-trigger-fdic-concerns>
Kelvin Chiu, founder of SilverCape Investments in Singapore, likes to hire talented traders who don't fit into traditional multi-strategy or hedge fund models. He finds them on social media and Substack. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/ex-goldman-trader-builds-mini-pod-shop-with-unconventional-hires?taid=6ab5b3a73a03d10001617da8&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Joseph Baratta, the head of private equity at Blackstone, is leaving the firm aged 55. This is seemingly because Jon Gray (56) is expected to become the next CEO. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/blackstones-top-private-equity-executive-is-preparing-to-leave-firm-6d7057db?mod=deals_news_article_pos1>
It sounds easy to get a graduate financial services job in Japan. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/japan-banks-hedge-funds-tussle-for-top-graduates-amid-jobs-boom?taid=6ab5de78abb846000197a391&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
EY has designed simulations to let junior staff practice asking clients for information or confronting a co-worker about a missed deadline. This is to compensate for the fact that AI now does this and juniors need practice. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/we-all-hated-busy-work-now-that-its-disappearing-it-turns-out-we-miss-it-d56bb48b?mod=e2tw>
Ben Rosen was an analyst at Morgan Stanley when he foresaw the growth of the personal computer in 1979. At conferences, he liked to balance chairs on his chin. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/tech/benjamin-rosen-wall-street-pcs-dead-c3600a73?mod=e2tw>
My husband never stops working. Should I leave him? (Guardian) <https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2026/sep/27/my-husband-never-stops-working-but-he-wont-discuss-it-should-i-leave-him>
“I’ve had men crying in my office who are desperate for jobs. They have put three kids through private school, often have large mortgages and they aren’t ready to give up on their careers. But no one will hire them.” (The Times) <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/27/londons-investment-bankers-lawyers-paid-more-than-1bn>

item.title: A Canadian bank in London is quietly building its rates team with some big hires
item.description:
Away from JPMorgan, macro traders are having a tough third quarter in both banks </news/macro-hedge-fund-losses> and funds </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>. There are sign that some market participants are using this to add dissatisfied talent.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Bank of Montreal (BMO) is among those quietly building. The Canadian bank quietly added Benjamin Storey, a trading veteran and the former head of rates sales at Bank of America in late July. Now we understand that it's also hired Fred Goulipian, the head of euroswaps trading at Natixis.
Goulipian didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. BMO declined to comment.
The European macro market has been short of talent for the past few years after an exodus of people to hedge funds. With some macro funds and pods now doing badly, there's always a possibility that some of these people might come back again. Samuele Grosso, for example, left HSBC for Taula Capital in Milan, before turning to banking to work with his old boss at BofA. </news/hsbc-trader-who-left-for-a-hedge-fund-quickly-joins-his-old-boss-at-a-us-bank>
Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and Nomura have all indicated that third quarter rates revenues in particular have been soft. JPMorgan, however, declared earlier this month that there had been "broad based" strength across its fixed income sales and trading business since July.
JPMorgan parted company with Pierre Morel, its former global co-head of macro credit trading in September 2025. Morel has recently arrived <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-02/jpmorgan-s-former-macro-credit-trading-co-head-joins-redhedge>at RedHedge Asset Management in London, where he, too, appears to be hiring.
